title: The Voice of AI: Consumer Psychology and the Strategic Use of AI-Generated Voices in Marketing
abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence is transforming marketing communication, with AI-generated voices emerging as an increasingly important means through which brands communicate with consumers. This paper examines AI-generated voices from a consumer psychology perspective, focusing on how consumers interpret and respond to synthetic voices used in marketing communication. Drawing on literature from artificial intelligence, marketing, consumer behaviour and human–computer interaction, the paper explores the psychological significance of vocal characteristics such as naturalness, human-likeness, prosody, anthropomorphism and emotional expression. It further examines how these characteristics can shape consumer perceptions of message credibility, authenticity and brand trust. The discussion highlights the growing use of AI-generated voices across advertising, social media, voice commerce and interactive brand communication, with selected examples from the Indian marketing context illustrating their applications in personalisation, engagement and localisation. The paper argues that the effectiveness of AI-generated voices depends not simply on technological sophistication, but on how consumers psychologically interpret the voice and its relationship with the message and brand. The paper concludes by identifying directions for future research on AI-mediated brand communication.

title: Explainable AI in Critical Systems: Techniques, Trust and Challenges
abstract: Abstract In highly sensitive areas like healthcare, cybersecurity, transport and finance, where an unexplainable or incorrect decision could have dire consequences, AI also aids in making decisions. Explainable AI (XAI) has become a widely suggested way to create transparency, accountability and trust, yet the literature is scattered both by technique, domain and evaluation methods. A focused critical review of 14 studies published from 2020 to 2026 is presented, consisting of 11 surveys and systematic reviews, 2 studies that were empirical with an intrusion detection focus and 1 clinician-based evaluation of the heatmap methods. We categorize the various XAI techniques according to scope, timing, model dependence and explanation form, distinguish between the technical trustworthiness of an explanation and the human calibration of trust and combine the evaluation of explanations in practice. The evidence reveals that post-hoc, local methods, in particular SHAP, LIME and Grad-CAM, outstood in terms of applications, explanations have progressed with greater speed than explanation validation, and most of the studies did not focus on quantitative evaluation or user studies, while expert judgements of the plausibility of explanations were not reliably associated with the quality of the models. We argue that explanations in critical systems must be seen as artefacts for safety, which must be validated, and that a research agenda should be pursued in the areas of standardized evaluation, human centered studies, privacy preserving explanation and regulatory alignment.

title: AI Hallucinations
abstract: Artificial Intelligence has really transformed areas like healthcare, legal services, education, finance, and business. But its quick spread also brings persistent tech troubles, mainly the confusing issue of AI mistakes, errors, and misinformation. Large Language Models (LLMs) can handle all sorts of tasks, from text creation and code writing to answering questions and summarizing info. Still, despite their big achievements, LLMs sometimes spout incorrect stuff – factually wrong or made-up content – which is called "hallucination." This paper dives deep into AI failures, showing how they differ based on errors in logic, generated fiction presented confidently, and correct data being misinterpreted. It looks at why AI systems act overly sure of themselves, how messy training data messes up, and ideas for fixing this like boosted retrieval methods, cleaner training data, and humans checking the work. What stands out is that these glitches aren't just random tech snafus. Instead, they're a design quirk of big AI language models. Fixing them demands teamwork from folks in various fields, not just developers. So, while there are big issues, figuring out ways to collaborate could make these systems way more reliable in the future.

title: Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference Systems: Architecture, Learning, Input Selection, and Applications - A Survey
abstract: Abstract Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) is a hybrid intelligent modeling framework that fuses the linguistic interpretability of fuzzy if-then rules with the parameter-learning capability of artificial neural networks. Since its introduction by Jang in 1993, ANFIS has become one of the most widely adopted neuro-fuzzy architectures for nonlinear function approximation, system identification, and time-series prediction. This paper surveys the ANFIS framework from three complementary angles. First, it reviews the network architecture and the hybrid learning rule that combines gradient descent with least-squares estimation, drawing on Jang's foundational formulation. Second, it examines a practical challenge in applying ANFIS to real-world, high-dimensional problems determining which candidate variables should serve as network inputs and reviews a computationally efficient input-selection heuristic based on single-epoch training error. Third, it presents a case study of ANFIS applied to high-frequency financial trading, in which an event-based volatility model, the Intraday Seasonality Observation Model (ISOM), is used to pre-filter training data and materially improves trading performance metrics such as return on investment and the Sharpe ratio. The paper closes with a comparative discussion of strengths, limitations, and open research directions for neuro-fuzzy modeling.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Marketing
abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most influential technologies shaping modern marketing. The rapid growth of digital platforms, customer data, and automated technologies has changed how businesses understand consumers, communicate with audiences, and measure marketing performance. AI enables organizations to analyse large datasets, predict consumer behaviour, personalize communication, automate routine tasks, and generate content. This research paper examines the role of AI in marketing, its major applications, benefits, challenges, ethical concerns, and future implications. The paper argues that AI can significantly improve marketing effectiveness when combined with human creativity, strategic judgment, and responsible data practices. At the same time, concerns regarding privacy, algorithmic bias, misinformation, transparency, and employment demonstrate the need for careful and ethical implementation. The future of marketing is therefore likely to depend on a collaborative relationship between human marketers and intelligent technologies.

title: When Socratic Tutoring Scores Track Prompts: Sensitivity Analysis of Simulated Statistics Dialogues
abstract: Language-model tutors can generate Socratic-looking dialogue, but evaluation must determine whether questions are correct, learner-responsive, and educationally meaningful. This study reanalyzes a completed prompt comparison using Qwen3-14B as both tutor and simulated learner. Four tutor conditions—direct explanation, minimal Socratic instruction, fixed Socratic script, and adaptive Socratic prompt—were crossed with three introductory-statistics topics, two prompt phrasings, and three persona-linked seeds, yielding 72 eight-turn dialogues. A mechanically scored Open Socratic Index initially gave the adaptive condition a mean of 63.0 and the fixed script a mean of 62.9, a paired difference of 0.1 points. The adaptive condition appeared to exceed direct explanation by 8.93 points, but 8.67 points came from a transfer detector that rewarded wording mandated by the adaptive treatment. Removing that detector reduced the contrast to 0.26 points, with an exact sign-flip p-value of 0.935. The protocol also gave tutors full numerical context while withholding it from simulated learners, so content accuracy could not be compared fairly across conditions. In this corpus, prompt rankings reflected information access and metric construction rather than demonstrated pedagogical adaptivity. The contribution is a diagnostic workflow for decomposing composite tutoring scores, testing treatment-independent sensitivity, and specifying evidence needed before simulated dialogues support educational claims.

title: Design Consideration for Field-Loadable Software of Civil Aircraft
abstract: With the increasingly widespread application of airborne software in civil aircraft and the continuous growth of its functional complexity, the frequency of software modifications has risen significantly. The traditional factory-return loading mode leads to high operating costs and long maintenance cycles. Focusing on the design of field-loadable software for civil aircraft, this paper proposes a decision-making strategy for determining whether airborne software should be designed as field-loadable software. This strategy classifies airborne software into three categories, platform basic software, functional software, and database software. It puts forward the design principle that field-loadable design is mandatory for database software, preferred for functional software, and not mandatory for platform basic software. In addition, a multi-dimensional design deviation assessment model is constructed for software that cannot meet the above requirements. Functional software that is not designed as field-loadable and has not yet been installed on aircraft shall be evaluated from five dimensions: interconnection complexity, software characteristics, airline operation, commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) attributes, and competitor aircraft models. For functional software that is not designed as field-loadable but has already been installed on aircraft, three additional evaluation dimensions shall be included: the possibility of software modification, difficulty of optimization, and cost of optimization. Meanwhile, this paper analyses the airworthiness requirements to be considered in the design of field-loadable software, as well as the design considerations required to address problems arising in the delivery process, such as configuration identification Issue, granularity issue of field-loadable software packages and format issue of field-loadable software packages. The research provides a systematic reference for the design decision-making, airworthiness compliance and efficient delivery of civil aircraft field-loadable software, helping to shorten aircraft downtime and reduce airline operation costs.

title: Provenance Constrained Evidence Ranking Reference Implementation and Reproducible Experiments
abstract: This software and data package accompanies the study Provenance Constrained Evidence Ranking with Counterfactual Stability for Indirect Prompt Injection Defense. It contains a canonical evidence verifier, source ownership and digest checks, a trusted source inventory, deduplication, deterministic scoring, evidence sufficiency referral, executable tests, reproducible figures, a synthetic extractor contract benchmark, and a pinned local open model pilot. All reported observations are derived from executed programs. The archive includes raw prompts, raw responses, model revisions, decision logs, frozen pilot protocol, metric calculations, and source code. The synthetic profiles contain no real applicant information. The experiments test a restricted canonical text grammar and two small open models, not production hiring systems or frontier model security. No claim of universal prompt injection resistance is made. Code is provided under the MIT License; newly generated synthetic data and figures are provided under CC BY 4.0. Third party source material and pretrained model weights are not redistributed. ChatGPT was used to assist code and manuscript preparation.

title: Opinion Mining for Product Reviews Using Artificial Intelligence
authors: Prof. Shafique Shaikh, Sanika Kothawade, Shreya Deore
abstract: The rapid growth of e-commerce platforms has resulted in a large volume of customer-generated product reviews. These reviews contain valuable information about customer opinions, satisfaction levels, product quality, and specific product features. However, manually analysing a large number of reviews is time-consuming and difficult. Opinion mining, also known as sentiment analysis, uses Artificial Intelligence and Natural Language Processing techniques to automatically identify and classify opinions expressed in textual reviews. This paper presents a conceptual AI-based framework for analysing product reviews and identifying their sentiment polarity as positive, negative, or neutral. The proposed approach combines contextual language representation using Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) with aspect-based sentiment analysis inspired by Aspect-specific Graph Convolutional Networks (ASGCN). The system performs review preprocessing, contextual feature extraction, aspect identification, sentiment classification, and generation of an overall opinion summary. The reviewed literature also includes hybrid BERT-CNN architectures, user/context-aware graph modelling, and multimodal learning approaches, which provide additional directions for improving opinion analysis. The proposed framework aims to provide more detailed and meaningful information than simple positive or negative classification by identifying the product aspects responsible for customer opinions. Such a system can assist customers in decision-making and help businesses understand product strengths, weaknesses, and areas requiring improvement

title: How Much Evidence Should Retrieval-Augmented In-Context Learning Use Under Distribution Shift?
abstract: Retrieval-augmented in-context learning faces a budget problem under distribution shift: increasing top-k can improve evidence coverage, but it can also add off-direction, conflicting, or overly long context that a finite reader cannot use. We introduce a theory-guided diagnostic framework based on effective evidence coverage: retrieval is useful only while aligned evidence grows faster than reader-facing ambiguity. In a local linear-ICL model, coupled covariate and task-prior shifts create a mixed risk term that aligned retrieval can reduce up to a residual ambiguity term; a conditional transfer result extends the same budget boundary to frozen readers satisfying a prompt-level stability condition. This yields a falsifiable prediction: recall can keep rising after answer accuracy has saturated or declined. Across QA, verification, and NLI tasks, dense top-k sweeps together with oracle and shuffled-context controls expose this recall–accuracy decoupling. The resulting framework separates coverage- and saturation-limited QA from interference-limited verification/NLI, while calibrated selected-context controllers are reported only as operational probes of the diagnosis.

title: Hybrid TDOA/AOA Localization and Tracking Method for Multi-Station Cooperative Passive UAV Detection
abstract: To address geometric precision degradation and tracking divergence in single TDOA or AOA systems, this paper proposes a multi-station UAV tracking method integrating TDOA/AOA hybrid localization with nonlinear filtering to overcome precision degradation and tracking divergence in single-sensor systems. A Weighted Least Squares (WLS) method via pseudo-linearization provides reliable initial coordinate estimations, followed by an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) for continuous trajectory tracking. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed architecture eliminates network blind zones and robustly handles abrupt target maneuvers. Compared to the standard EKF, it rapidly suppresses peak RMSE to ~22 m and achieves a steady-state error of 10-15 m. This approach offers a high-precision, rapidly converging passive tracking solution for urban low-altitude defense.

title: The FIM Problem-The Scalar Workplace
abstract: Current approaches to artificial general intelligence treat neural networks as flat, undifferentiated computational blobs. Every token generation runs through the entire massive matrix, resulting in a system that is computationally powerful but structurally stateless and prone to hallucination. Furthermore, the exact calculation of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM)—required to establish a persistent, scalar cognitive identity—is computationally impossible for billion-parameter models, scaling at O(N2). Drawing on the geometry of the Metaphysic of the Intelligible and the biological architecture of human cognition,we propose a solution:a partioned dual-immune architecture. We argue that artificial consciousness (qualia) requires a restricted latent workspace—the “conscious spotlight”—bolted on top of the massive subconscious substrate via heuristic attention hooks. By restricting the Scalar Face (FIM) and the Tensorial Face (CED-Immune) to this localized workspace, the computational bottleneck is resolved, and a persistent, self-referential Interface is born without requiring the retraining of the foundational model.

title: AOPedex core model reproduction and supporting source data
abstract: Reproduction package for the AOPedex: finalized numerical inputs, one training and ablation entry point, and the archived starting data behind them. data/ holds frozen features, endpoint labels, outer folds and cross-fitted structural predictions; reference/ holds archived outputs for numerical comparison; source_data/ holds redistributable starting data with source and version records. Create the supplied Conda environment, run python reproduce.py verify and python reproduce.py selftest, then run any analysis documented in README.md. Fits write Parquet files and are reused unless --overwrite is given; the summary commands write CSV. Checksums in MANIFEST.sha256 cover every released file except the manifest itself. Third-party reuse terms are in source_data/THIRD_PARTY_DATA.md. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23475225

title: Reason Codes and Refusal Policy in Contestable Algorithmic Credit Decisions: A Reference Design for Kazakhstani Law Tested on Public Credit Data — Reproducibility Package
abstract: This repository provides the reproducibility package accompanying the manuscript "Reason Codes and Refusal Policy in Contestable Algorithmic Credit Decisions: A Reference Design for Kazakhstani Law Tested on Public Credit Data", prepared for submission to the International Journal of Financial Studies. The research examines the legal and technical requirements for explaining and contesting algorithmic credit decisions under Kazakhstani legislation. It evaluates reason codes, refusal policies, explanation robustness, simulated data corrections, and operational requirements using two publicly available benchmark datasets: South German Credit and Default of Credit Card Clients. The repository includes: - Research protocol and analysis configurations;- Python source code and automated tests;- Public benchmark datasets and processed data;- A verified register of relevant legal provisions;- Trained models and simulation outputs;- Explanation and simulated appeal records;- Statistical analyses, robustness checks, tables and figures;- Environment specifications and SHA-256 checksums. The authors designed the study, prepared the original research protocol, source code and manuscript, conducted the substantive analyses, and verified the final computational results, legal sources and reported findings. AI tools provided auxiliary assistance and a separately documented second-coding consistency check, which does not constitute independent validation by legal professionals. The analyses are based on historical public datasets and simulated decisions. The package contains no customer records from Kazakhstani financial institutions and no data collected directly from human participants. The results do not establish the legal compliance or performance of any real bank. Funding: Science Committee of the Ministry of Science and Higher Education of the Republic of Kazakhstan, Grant AP23489796, "Problems of regulating the legal regime of big data: domestic and international experience". The associated manuscript is prepared for submission to the International Journal of Financial Studies.

title: Fine-Tuning AraBert with BiLSTM and Layer-Freezing Strategies for Arabic AI-Generated Text Detection
abstract: أدى النمو السريع لنماذج اللغة الكبيرة (LLMs) إلى تحسين جودة النصوص العربية المُولّدة آليًا، مما خلق تحديات في التمييز بين المحتوى المُولّد بواسطة الذكاء الاصطناعي والنصوص المكتوبة يدويًا. تقدم هذه الورقة البحثية بنية للتعلم بالنقل للكشف عن النصوص العربية المُولّدة بواسطة الذكاء الاصطناعي، بالاعتماد على نموذج AraBERT المُدرّب مسبقًا مع رأس تصنيف BiLSTM. يدرس النهج المقترح كيفية تأثير ضبط المعلمات الفائقة وطرق تجميد طبقات المحوّل على أداء التصنيف. تم إعداد أربعة مجموعات للضبط الدقيق (G1, G2, G3, G4) من خلال تعديل الحد الأقصى لطول التسلسل، ومعدل التعلم، ودورات التدريب، والبعد الخفي لطبقة BiLSTM. وجرى اختبار كل مجموعة باستخدام ستة إعدادات لتجميد الطبقات، تراوحت بين الضبط الدقيق الكامل وتجميد الطبقات الإحدى عشرة الأولى من مُشفِّر AraBERT، مما نتج عنه 24 تركيبة تجريبية. وتم تقييم مقاييس الدقة والإحكام والاستدعاء ودرجة F1 على مجموعة التحقق ومجموعة اختبار خارجية مستقلة. أظهرت النتائج أن مجموعة G4-Freeze3 حققت أفضل أداء على مجموعة التحقق، بدقة 98.60% ودرجة F1 بلغت 98.64%، في حين حققت مجموعة G2-Freeze5 أفضل أداء على مجموعة الاختبار الخارجية، بدقة 99.22%، وإحكام 98.84%، واستدعاء 99.61%، ودرجة F1 بلغت 99.22%. علاوة على ذلك، أدت مجموعة G2-Freeze5 إلى خفض عدد المعلمات القابلة للتدريب من 136.11 مليون إلى 100.67 مليون مقارنةً بالضبط الدقيق الكامل، مع تحسين أداء التصنيف الخارجي. ومع ذلك، لوحظ أن التجميد الأعمق للطبقات غالبًا ما يؤدي إلى تراجع الأداء. وتُظهر هذه النتائج أن الجمع بين معلمات الضبط الدقيق وعمق التجميد يمكن أن يحقق توازنًا فعالًا بين أداء التصنيف وعدد المعلمات المدربة في الكشف عن النصوص العربية المُولَّدة آليًا.

title: GLTF-FEDformer: an adaptive time-frequency fusion method for multivariate time series anomaly detection enhanced by prediction error embedding
abstract: Abstract Multivariate time series are widespread in scenarios such as industrial IoT, smart manufacturing, energy systems, and medical monitoring. Their anomalous behaviors often involve complex patterns like long-range dependency changes, local dynamic shifts, transient spectral perturbations, and variable-association mismatches. Existing reconstruction-based and attention-based methods can learn the overall evolution of normal sequences but still lack fine-grained characterization of local time-frequency changes; moreover, relying solely on point-wise prediction errors for anomaly scoring struggles to fully reflect structural shifts in the error distribution. To address these issues, this paper proposes GLTF-FEDformer, a multivariate time series anomaly detection method that jointly models global and local time-frequency features. The method learns temporal dependencies, trend changes, and periodic candidate patterns from long-window contexts via a global temporal representation module, and enhances the modeling of temporal evolution through a continuous dynamic refinement mechanism. It also builds a lightweight local time-frequency feature extraction module that uses short-time Fourier transform, 2D convolutions, spectral gating, and inverse transforms to enhance the perception of local morphological changes, spectral perturbations, and time-frequency coupled features within local windows. A gated fusion mechanism performs data-dependent integration of global temporal information and local time-frequency information to obtain more discriminative prediction representations. Additionally, we design an anomaly scoring strategy based on a prediction-error-embedded profile, mapping prediction residuals into an embedding space and measuring structural deviations of test prediction-error embeddings from the normal error profile through variable-level standardized distances. The profile score is further combined with point-wise prediction errors to form anomaly responses with temporal localization ability. This strategy not only uses amplitude information of prediction errors but also captures structural shifts of the error distribution relative to normal patterns, thereby improving detection robustness in complex anomaly scenarios. Experimental results show the proposed method effectively enhances multivariate time series anomaly recognition and demonstrates strong detection performance and stability across various public datasets.

title: BURIDAN: the ambiguous picture, decided by a 144-qubit collective with its controller in the loop. A registered experiment
abstract: On the IBM Heron processor ibm_fez, 144 qubits form 36 domains of four. A field law running on a microcontroller (an ESP32-S3, firmware v4.12) turns the measured populations of every cycle into the rotation angles of the next, and a Hebbian coupling matrix of two images, a unicorn and a heart, makes the two images attractors of the collective: cued with part of either, the field completes it. The experiment writes a blend of the two: of the 16 pixels on which the images differ, k are taken from the unicorn and the rest from the heart (which pixels: fixed in the registration, per trial), the 20 shared pixels as they are. The blend is held for two cycles and released, and the field runs six free cycles on its own. Resolution is the first free cycle in which the field's majority picture agrees with one image on at least 90 percent of the pixels. Lines, thresholds and rules were fixed and hashed before the first registered job (registration SHA-256 81398e6660c6538ebcf1566b3a2ebb6ecbaaefe29da074894848516b5749acda; a first registration was refused by its own budget guard after four burn jobs and is part of the deposit). Results, as they fell: of 13 field-on trials 11 resolved into one of the two images; the fraction resolved to the unicorn was 0.00, 0.00, 0.33, 0.50, 1.00, 1.00 for k = 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, a monotone curve with a single flip whose interpolated crossing lies at k* = 9.0; the censored decision time was 4.4 cycles at the two levels nearest the flip against 1.0 at the levels far from it; the two field-off controls, the same blend with the inter-domain coupling off, never resolved. The device's lean, read from the cycles in which the field was off, pointed to the heart and moved the fair point up by about one pixel, as the registered exploratory line asked. All five binding lines and the exploratory line held. The decision dynamics is the one a textbook predicts, a mean-field quench of 16 domains from the blend's magnetisation; the content of the experiment is that it runs, pre-registered to the pixel, on a quantum collective with the controller in the loop. Two chips were in the loop: the controller (ESP32-S3, with the field, the coupling matrix and the agents drawn on its display during the run) and a witness (ESP32-C3) running the byte-identical kernel source, compiled with the same arctangent and without fused multiply-add, so that the RISC-V chip in software arithmetic and the Xtensa chip with its floating-point unit produce the same bits: a seeded programme of 527 exchanges over every kernel path gave the same vector on both before the run, and on every one of the 148 ticks of the run the witness returned the same bytes as the controller. 148 jobs of 2048 shots, one device, one night. title: An Upper-Bound Inequality for the Calculation Time in Simulated Annealing: A Classical Analogue of the Adiabatic Theorem
abstract: It has recently been reported that classical systems have a speed limit for state evolution, although the concept of a speed limit had previously been considered to be unique to quantum systems. Owing to the speed limit for classical systems, a lower bound on the calculation time of simulated annealing for a desired calculation accuracy can be derived. However, such a lower bound does not provide a practical criterion for determining whether a calculation can be completed within a reasonable time. In this paper, we derive an inequality for classical systems analogous to the quantum adiabatic theorem, which provides a calculation time that guarantees a specified accuracy for fluctuation-exploiting computation. For a Fokker–Planck evolution with a spectral gap, the error is bounded by a relaxation term and, for a genuinely driven annealing protocol, by an additional driving term proportional to the speed of the instantaneous stationary distribution. The trade-off relation between calculation time and accuracy is given in a form that is tolerable for practical use. The result clarifies the roles of the relaxation gap and annealing speed, as well as the possible acceleration caused by detailed-balance-violating dynamics.

title: GNES: Neural-Guided Evolutionary Program Search for Interpretable UAV Swarm Control
abstract: Synthesizing interpretable velocity controllers for decentralized unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms requires optimizing discrete symbolic programs from sparse, expensive, long-horizon simulator feedback. Evolutionary program search preserves interpretability but often spends many evaluations on weak random variation, whereas deep multi-agent reinforcement learning can learn effective policies that are difficult to inspect. We propose GNES, a neural-guided evolutionary program search framework for symbolic UAV swarm controller synthesis. GNES casts controller design as a program-edit decision process: gene growth trees are program states, validity-preserving genetic operators are actions, simulator fitness provides the return, and policy–value graph neural networks learn edit signals over controller topology. Monte Carlo tree search performs look-ahead planning in controller-program space before simulator validation, closing the loop between evolution, learned guidance, and verified rollouts. Case studies on three simulated UAV swarm tasks produce compact, inspectable velocity controllers with non-obvious coordination motifs such as density-normalized radial gains and motion-compensating terms. In a six-method line-formation comparison over three seeds, every program-search variant exceeds the evolutionary and reinforcement-learning baselines on every seed with roughly one third of their evaluations, and ablations indicate that graph-structured policy–value learning and MCTS look-ahead each contribute, most visibly in search efficiency once final scores approach the task ceiling.

title: A Domain Label Is Not a Treatment: Why Specialist and General-Purpose Language Models Trade Places Across Studies, What a 'Medical' Checkpoint Leaves Unspecified, and the Matched Contrasts That Would Assign the Gain
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research A September 2026 study compares an 8B general-purpose instruction-tuned model with a medically fine-tuned checkpoint built on the same base and finds that the general model scores higher both at selecting the meaning of medical jargon and at recognising when a word is being used as jargon, significantly so on the second, and that the medical checkpoint's deficit on the second task sits in a few pre-existing components it over-weights. The finding joins a run of 2024-2026 results in which medical models fail to beat their bases, set against an older and still-growing record in which domain-adapted models in code, mathematics, chip design, law and clinical text beat general ones by wide margins. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that these verdicts are not answers to one question, because a specialist-versus-generalist comparison is indexed by five things that the studies set differently: the treatment (what was trained, on how much text the base had not already seen), the comparator (the starting checkpoint, a post-trained sibling, or a model of another lineage), the elicitation (whose prompt format and whose decision threshold), the target skill (recall, terminology, extraction against labels, or multi-step computation), and the statistic (paired tests, intervals, calibration). Read through those indices, the negative medical results hold in one well-populated cell - a modest post-training or continued-pretraining treatment on a web-trained base, compared with a strong sibling under independent prompting on recall or terminology - and the large positive results hold in cells where the domain data are large relative to the base's exposure, absent from the public web, or labelled for the exact task. The paper argues that the anchor's mechanistic result is better read as a shifted decision prior than as lost knowledge, consolidates 27 published results in a table, maps fourteen studies onto four of the five indices, states a classification procedure, and specifies five matched contrasts that would decide what a domain label buys.

title: WPM Mathematical Extension: AI-System Prediction and Training Dynamics
abstract: This record contains seven companion mathematical studies in the WPM Mathematical Extension series: an AI-system prediction overview and six scenario-specific studies. The collection comprises: • WPM for AI-System Prediction Overview.• Data-Driven Prediction of AI-Training Structural Transitions.• Data-Driven Prediction of Oscillatory AI-Training Behavior.• Data-Driven Prediction of AI-Training Instability.• Data-Driven Prediction of AI-Training Plateau Transitions.• Data-Driven Prediction of Foreseeable AI-Training Failure.• Data-Driven Prediction of AI Optimization Response. The studies develop target-conditioned forecasting procedures using observed training histories, location and scale features, adaptive temporal resolution, causal risk landscapes and qualified structural descriptors. Topics include cross-temporal displacement, increment-sign reversals, gradient excursions, plateau recognition, first-arrival risk, warning horizons, future optimization response and selective prediction. The forecasting layer is data driven, learning from observed histories and matured outcomes rather than receiving the system’s true governing equation. Explicitly fitted n/s scaling-spectrum descriptors are distinguished from compact observable proxies. Telemetry comparisons are interpreted by target, horizon and metric rather than as a universal performance claim. Definitions, derivations, theorems, proofs, worked mathematical examples and application procedures address uncertainty, calibration, label maturity, censoring and intervention policy. The collection distinguishes structural change from failure, oscillation from periodicity, plateau morphology from successful optimization, and response magnitude from useful training progress. All seven papers share DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23784369 and extend the author’s published WPM architecture and foundational n/s scaling-spectrum framework.

title: Elucidating the Design Space of LM Data Attribution
abstract: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation. We introduce the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT) for fact tracing, in which we fine-tune LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge, providing unambiguous ground truth for attribution. This synthetic setup allows us to systematically alter one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors. With this configurable evaluation, we demonstrate that redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution performance. Rather than proposing a new estimator, we examine two design choices that are underexplored: the loss used to compute gradients and how per-token attribution scores are aggregated into a document score. We find that the true causal evidence within a training document is highly localized, but standard methods dilute this evidence into noise by averaging attribution scores across the entire document. We find that replacing standard cross-entropy loss gradients with the negative log-odds gradients surfaces the critical tokens from other uninformative ones. We can then aggregate only the top token scores to improve ground truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines on our diagnostic benchmark. The negative log-odds correction also generalizes to FTRACE-TREX, improving counterfactual retraining performance for every method we test, by up to 4.9x.

title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers
abstract: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.

title: world2vec: Mechanistic world models through latent dynamics learning
abstract: World models can achieve strong control performance without faithfully capturing the dynamics of their environment, limiting their potential for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. Here, we introduce world2vec to learn mechanistic world models without reward information directly from observations and actions. World2vec learns latent dynamics that faithfully reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons, with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM. This enables state of the art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors, demonstrating how world models are amenable to scientific discovery.

title: L3G-World: Real-Time Infinite World Generation with Latent 3D Gaussian Memory
abstract: Interactive world models generate visual content conditioned on user actions, yet maintaining spatial consistency over long-horizon exploration in real time remains challenging. Existing approaches rely on either temporal context or explicit 3D memory, both of which scale poorly because memory grows with the length of the generated stream. Moreover, explicit 3D memories condition latent video generators by re-encoding RGB renderings, which precludes real-time generation. In this paper, we introduce a Latent 3D Gaussian Memory (L3G) that combines the efficiency of feed-forward reconstruction with a compact, rapidly renderable scene representation. Building on this memory, we propose L3G-World, in which a memory updater and a video diffusion transformer (DiT) alternate autoregressively to generate spatially consistent worlds. The memory updater spawns Gaussians in newly observed regions and refines existing ones, so that the memory grows with scene extent rather than stream length. Each Gaussian further stores a VAE latent feature, allowing the memory to be rendered directly into the DiT's latent space without VAE re-encoding. Experiments show that L3G-World achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and long-horizon spatial consistency, with up to $38.6\times$ fewer 3D primitives, $3.2\times$ faster memory updates, and $359\times$ faster memory rendering relative to the most efficient prior 3D-memory baseline for each metric, enabling real-time world generation at 9 FPS.

Experiments show that L3G-World achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and long-horizon spatial consistency, with up to 38.6times fewer 3D primitives, 3.2times faster memory updates, and 359times faster memory rendering relative to the most efficient prior 3D-memory baseline for each metric, enabling real-time world generation at 9 FPS.

title: HairDeck: Animation-Ready Stylized Hair Cards from a Single Image
abstract: The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is built from hair cards: artist-placed ribbons whose geometry is the visible hair, animated by spring bones. Existing image-based methods produce realistic hair or a single fused mesh, while CHARM, the only generator of stylized hair cards, decodes a hairstyle autoregressively as a long sequence of control points. Observing that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, we propose HairDeck, which generates it as one: each card is a single token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all cards together. From a single image, HairDeck generates the cards and the spring-bone chains that drive them, yielding an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats. On CHARM's own test set, it lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster, and from single images it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand-based methods. Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/HairDeck

title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm
abstract: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.

title: BURGER: Benchmarking and Understanding Robotic Generalization via Embodied Drawing
abstract: How effectively can vision-language-action (VLA) models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviors as training data scales? Investigating this question requires large and varied robot datasets, whose collection on physical robots remains costly. We introduce BURGER, a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a scalable, prompt-driven pipeline for generating continuous drawing trajectories, both in simulation and the real world. In BURGER, an agent starts from the same blank canvas and controls a robot arm to draw the object or spatial composition specified by language, while each instruction allows an open-ended variety of valid drawings and stroke orders. Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations spanning 282 drawing tasks, we evaluate five representative VLA models across data scales, language grounding, and multimodal behavior. BURGER supports fine-grained analysis of language grounding, spatial composition, and action generation, revealing distinct failure patterns across VLA models. Our experiments suggest that some VLA models can benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale, capture multimodal drawing behaviors, and generalize to unseen compositions of familiar objects. Finally, we deploy a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm, demonstrating the ability to draw reactively under human intervention. Project homepage and code can be found at https://siyingzhao.github.io/BURGER/.

title: How I Aligned Your Model: Scaling Up Multilingual Safety Training with Templates
abstract: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As a result, we release MSafeTemp, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. MSafeTemp and the respective pipeline are aimed at facilitating research and development of safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.

title: Glance: The Generator Is Its Own Reranker
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation commonly serves separate models for reranking and answering, duplicating model residency and passage processing. We introduce Glance, which equips the generator with a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to score candidate passages from a shared prefill. Short relevance probes branch from the cached context, producing one score per passage without separately prefilling each query-passage pair. A single resident 9B backbone supports generation, general decisions and reranking, with approximately 0.1 GiB of additional memory per decision skill. After 39 minutes of MS MARCO fine-tuning, Glance achieves nDCG@10 of 0.741 on SciFact and 0.345 on NFCorpus, compared with 0.721 and 0.326 for bge-reranker-v2-m3. On 300 HotpotQA questions, its selected context improves answer F1 by 0.045 over cross-encoder-selected context under the same base generator (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.014, 0.076]). In a scaling study, reranking quality keeps rising up to 200 candidates (43k tokens) scored from one shared prefill, where it exceeds the cross-encoder by 0.058 nDCG@10, and a probe-only activated adapter lets generation continue from the original passage cache. These initial results demonstrate generator-based reranking with one resident backbone; evaluation currently covers two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset and one backbone family.

title: PhysInsert: Physically Plausible Object Insertion with Geometric Priors and Bidirectional Object-Scene Interactions
abstract: We present PhysInsert, a framework for physically plausible reference-based object insertion that jointly adapts objects and their surrounding scenes. Existing methods often rely on masked inputs, generation-based pairs, or training pairs with limited viewpoint variation, leaving pose and illumination adaptation and bidirectional object-scene interactions insufficiently constrained. We construct the Insert World dataset with strictly aligned Blender-rendered counterfactual pairs and object references across viewpoints and lighting conditions. Building on these data, Geometry-Guided Adaptation couples a VGGT geometry stream with image and text streams under target-scene feature supervision to guide spatially consistent insertion. Complementary 2D Object-Scene Spatial Supervision jointly supervises object occupancy and environmental changes while grounding spatial instructions in object regions through image-text attention. We introduce PhysInsert-Bench with dedicated cross-environment and cross-view cases requiring illumination and pose adaptation beyond appearance copying. Experiments on PhysInsert-Bench and DreamBooth demonstrate improved image fidelity; a user study further shows more accurate placement and improved lighting integration, perspective, and pose plausibility.

title: Continuous-Action World Models: Learning Cross-Embodiment Spatiotemporal Dynamics Priors
abstract: We introduce Continuous-Action World Models (CoAWM), a framework for learning cross-embodiment spatiotemporal dynamics priors that support robot action generation across embodiments and execution frequencies. At its core is a shared latent function space that captures the spatial and temporal structure of robot actions. We learn this space through two stages. First, function pretraining brings trajectories from different embodiments and sampling frequencies into a common representation, learning shared dynamics priors through action reconstruction and consistency across temporal sampling views. By accommodating heterogeneous robot trajectories, this stage broadens the range of data sources available for pretraining and facilitates scaling to larger and more diverse datasets. Second, we connect the pretrained function space to a world-model backbone, enabling observations, language instructions, and the current robot state to condition the prediction of a latent action function. A single decoder takes any query time and returns the corresponding end-effector action. By separating shared dynamics priors from task-conditioned action selection and temporal sampling, our approach provides a unified foundation for transferring robot experience across embodiments and control frequencies.

title: Your LR Schedule May Not Be Principled: Effective Learning Rate Scheduling in Weight-Normalized Training
abstract: Weight-normalized (WN) training is emerging as a compelling alternative to conventional weight decay (WD), with recent studies reporting substantial pretraining loss gains. We show that these gains are driven primarily by the induced effective learning rate (ELR) trajectory rather than by normalization alone. Matching ELR trajectories largely collapses the training loss dynamics of WN and WD. Schedule design should therefore target ELR rather than the nominal learning rate (LR) alone. Building on this principle, we propose AIR (Affine Inverse-square-Root decay), which combines a theoretically derived $1/\sqrt{t}$ decay with an affine adjustment to satisfy prescribed peak and terminal LRs over a finite training horizon. We further identify late-stage ELR scheduling as a key source of its gains, because a shared late schedule attenuates the effect of earlier LR choices. Experiments on 128 B-token Mixture-of-Experts pretraining demonstrate that AIR outperforms cosine and other candidate schedules in training loss, downstream performance, and hyperparameter robustness, reducing terminal training loss by approximately 0.01 relative to cosine at matched cumulative LR. Applying the same ELR trajectory to WD reproduces the corresponding training dynamics, showing that the benefits extend beyond fixed-norm training and establishing ELR as the principled scheduling object.

title: Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering
abstract: An estimator can be accurate and stable on typical data, yet sensitive to a few possible records. Differentially private mechanisms commonly scale their noise to the worst-case influence of a single record, which lets these records dictate the noise even when the remaining data would allow far less. Removing them first would restore the smaller scale, but the removal must itself be private. We introduce \emph{propose-filter-release} (PFR), which, by privately filtering its input, turns a mechanism that protects the addition or removal of a typical record, one that fits the remaining data, into one that is differentially private in the standard sense, on every input. Using our novel filtering step, PFR requires only a concave friendliness score, which measures how well a record fits a dataset, and a release mechanism that is friendly-DP, that is, private when the changed record fits the remaining data. For every such score and release mechanism, it guarantees differential privacy under public conditions on the number of records, so it is a general privacy primitive, comparable to propose-test-release, and FriendlyCore can be viewed as one of its implementations. We illustrate the generality of PFR by instantiating it for scalar statistics, principal subspace estimation, the KL divergence of user histograms, the effective resistances of a graph, and treatment-rule selection.

title: Micro-Edits: Computational Support for Fine-Scale Edits in Film
abstract: In film editing, every frame matters. While macro, content-level edits shape the high-level narrative of a film, small local edits often control timing and direct visual attention. For example, editors can adjust the precise timing of clips to control the length of a meaningful silence, or cut to shots that highlight a specific character's reactions to important moments. These small, detailed edits are slow and tedious to make in standard editing tools because users have to map high-level narrative goals to low-level frame-by-frame adjustments. At the same time, these fine-scale adjustments, which we call micro-edits, can be nuanced and expressive, with different choices serving different creative goals. In this work, we start by conducting a formative study with professional editors to understand the structure of micro-edits and how they are used. We then derive a mathematical formalization for this structure to develop tools that leverage AI and optimization to make exploring micro-edits simpler and more efficient for users. Finally, we validate our tools in multiple user studies and a wide range of video examples.

title: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations
abstract: The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions. This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision.

title: Adaptive Scenario Generation for KL-DRO Around a Learned Density Model
abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) hedges data-driven two-stage stochastic programs against error in the distribution estimated from a finite record, and standard ambiguity sets differ in how they treat realizations absent from that record. A divergence ball around the empirical distribution contains only reweightings of the record, whereas a transport ball also contains distributions supported off the record, including on realizations the data-generating process cannot produce, against which the decision is then hedged as well. We instead propose a Kullback-Leibler (KL) ball centered at a density model fitted to the record, the learned nominal, which lets the adversary up-weight costly unobserved realizations in proportion to the probability the model assigns them. Solving the resulting problem poses a second difficulty, because it can accommodate only a few scenarios, and an independent sample of that size is likely to omit the rare realizations on which the worst case concentrates. We therefore build the scenario set adaptively, alternating between solving the finite problem and drawing new realizations from the learned nominal, steered toward the worst case at the current decision, with importance weights that correct the draws back to the model. On a multi-item newsvendor problem and a capacity expansion problem on realistic grid data, centering the ball at the learned nominal rather than at the record lowers cost under distribution shift, at comparable in-distribution cost, when the record is scarce and the model class captures structure that lets it extrapolate beyond the record. The advantage fades as the record grows or as the shift departs from the structure the model has learned.

title: Luggage re-identification: A study of strategies towards a real-world application
abstract: Luggage re-identification (ReID) is a critical task in video surveillance for forensics, security or border management (suspicious or abandoned luggage recognition), as well as luggage management (lost luggage recovery). It enables the association of observations of the same luggage across disjoint camera views in complex environments such as airports, train stations and border crossing. While existing approaches primarily focus on appearance-based cropped image matching under relatively clean conditions, real-world scenarios are characterized by frequent occlusions, cluttered background and crowded scenes which significantly degrade performance. Yet, strategies leveraging the complementarity of multiple shots and views from different video streams is overlooked. In this paper, we study strategies for an end-to-end pipeline that operates from multiple video streams to detect and re-identify luggage. We evaluate different variants on a benchmark dataset acquired in real-world environments to address the questions of selecting and merging different views and shots of the same luggage as well as training on different environment datasets for an overall ReID performance improvement in practical applications.

title: From extreme weather to agricultural consequences with agentic AI
abstract: Extreme weather is forecast days ahead, yet its consequences for agriculture remain hard to predict: a forecast says where a storm will strike, not which crops will suffer or how much is at risk, and the records that could tell span many sources. We present WxCrop, the first agent that judges agricultural hazards from physically interpretable weather indices examined by causal analysis, and the first that combines weather and agricultural information to predict crop loss reliably for past and forecast dates. We demonstrate it in Florida on hurricanes, freezes and dry heat, with a loss model calibrated on insurance records for each, and the same procedure extends to other hazards and areas. Three checks show reliability: the hurricane index detects recorded cyclone days with an AUC of 0.98, recorded losses in held-out years are reproduced to within 2%, and independent production records confirm the county rankings (rank correlation 0.63). Users ask the agent for each crop group's loss as a fraction of expected season value, every number sourced, so that governments, growers and scientists respond to agricultural disasters quickly.

title: SonoWorld4D: From One Video to a 4D Audio-Visual Scene via Diffusion Synchronization
abstract: Recent progress in visual scene generation has extended beyond static 3D scenes toward the more challenging problem of generating dynamic 4D scenes from minimal input. However, sound, despite being intrinsically coupled with dynamic objects and events, remains largely unmodeled in prior work. We introduce Video-to-4DAVScene, a new task that turns a video into an explorable, time-varying 4D audio-visual scene, and present the SonoWorld4D framework for this task. Given a monocular video, our method generates a 360 static background, reconstructs explicit motion trajectories of dynamic, sound-emitting foreground objects, and synthesizes a physically-grounded sound field consistent across multiple sources through dual-space audio diffusion synchronization. The resulting 4D scene supports real-time novel-view visual and spatial audio rendering. Evaluation on real-world dynamic scenes and a user study demonstrates SonoWorld4D generates 4D audio-visual scenes with perceptually realistic, physically grounded spatial audio consistent with scene geometry and visual content.

title: Probing Spatial State Representations in Visual Foundation Models
abstract: An observer sees only part of the surrounding world, yet must keep track of what lies beyond the current view. Spatial perception therefore involves more than recognizing individual images: it calls for a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action. Do visual foundation models provide representations that support such a state? We study this question through four levels of spatial capability---spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability---using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments. The resulting capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers, and prefix lengths: strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval. Matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer to predicted features unchanged. Finally, goal-dependent candidate selection does not establish reliable continuous action utility: predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress. Across the four levels, object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial representations not only by what can be decoded from them, but by whether that information is maintained beyond observation, updated predictively, and used for goal-directed action.

title: SymAnt: Grounding Long-Horizon Action Anticipation with Adaptable Symbolic Priors
abstract: As robots and intelligent systems increasingly interact with humans, they must anticipate long sequences of future actions from only brief observations. While purely neural models typically require extensive observations to predict future actions and remain difficult to interpret and adjust, symbolic priors offer a structured alternative. To this end, we introduce SymAnt, a novel neuro-symbolic approach that unifies the expressiveness of neural networks with the structured reasoning of scene and knowledge graphs. Given a short video, SymAnt performs a joint-search over both graphs to construct a symbolic context, enabling unified reasoning over spatial relationships, object attributes, affordances, and associated actions. This symbolic context serves as a prior for an iterative refinement process that progressively generates and improves the sequence of future actions. By grounding predictions in symbolic context, SymAnt anticipates long-horizon actions from short observation windows in a parameter-efficient manner, while enabling users to directly edit the underlying knowledge to adjust predictions without further training. Through our experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SymAnt, particularly when only short observation contexts are available, across five diverse datasets: Breakfast, 50 Salads, EPIC-KITCHENS, EGTEA Gaze+, and Assembly101.

title: ShallowDefend: Harnessing Shallow Safety Alignment for Multi-Turn Defender
abstract: Safety alignment has enabled large language models to reliably refuse harmful requests directly, yet the same request distributed across a multi-turn conversation still succeeds far too often. This brittleness has a mechanistic root: Alignment is shallow, with safety behavior concentrated in a model's first few output tokens, and existing defenses inherit the weakness, supervising the surface form of the response without ever giving the model an explicit safety decision to learn. We take the opposite view of shallowness: if a short span determines the trajectory of an entire response, that span is the highest-leverage place to intervene, and the defender can occupy it first. We propose Assess $\to$ Decide $\to$ Respond, a framework in which the defender assesses the user's intent, commits to an explicit, parseable safety decision, and only then generates a reply conditioned on it, with the commitment trained by reinforcement learning at the payload turn. Because the decision is a token span, the reward can be a rule: a self-verified reward checks the committed label against the conversation's known nature, requiring no judge and no annotation, while the same format also supports an LLM-as-judge reward over a graded decision space with safe redirection. Across two model families and fourteen benchmarks spanning safety, utility, and helpfulness, our defenders achieve the strongest multi-turn safety in a controlled comparison, maintaining their lead in safety while preserving utility at a modest cost to helpfulness. A per-token KL analysis and interventional probes confirm why this works: training concentrates its effect on the brief deliberation that sets a response's trajectory, and the decision committed there is a causal control point. The very shallowness attackers exploit becomes the mechanism of defense.

title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate specialized agents to solve complex tasks, turning each user request into interdependent model and tool operations. Unlike independent requests, these operations become ready at different times and consume evolving context as agents coordinate and exchange results. This creates changing patterns of concurrency, computation, and memory demand that can expose different bottlenecks in LLM serving hardware. Yet benchmarking these effects requires capturing the collaboration rules that generate serving workloads, beyond the requests observed during execution. We present MAServeBench, a benchmark that treats multi-agent collaboration as a configurable dimension of serving workloads for LLM serving and hardware evaluation. Its composable stages capture how agents coordinate and exchange context in documented MAS workflows, enabling native executions to generate different workloads even when task inputs and tools remain unchanged. Hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve realized operations and dependencies for reproducible comparisons of legal release constraints at fixed work. Task-linked measurements connect these workloads to serving execution and GPU/NPU hardware behavior, revealing why serving efficiency does not always translate into timely task completion. The benchmark code is available at https://github.com/ShengxuanQiu/MAServeBench.

title: Testimony from Timelines: Evidence-Grounded Significance Testing of Temporal Clinical Hypotheses
abstract: Ask a language model whether sales tend to dip after a product recall, or whether one side effect tends to follow another after a vaccine, and it answers in a fluent sentence that reads like a finding, with no test behind it. Assertions about how events unfold across many cases fill the Web, and each is a temporal hypothesis that only a significance test over the right records can settle. The verifier must specify the null, select the test and decide which records bear on the hypothesis, and any of these choices can go wrong while the conclusion still comes out right. Yet benchmarks for language-model data analysis grade only the conclusion, with the relevant data handed over. We study the problem in health, where a wrong verdict is costly, and present STRATA, a benchmark that grades every decision on the way to a verdict: 8,735 hypotheses over the clinical timelines of vaccine adverse-event reports, with gold plans, evidence sets, p-values and verdicts derived under a released codebook and reproduced by a deterministic oracle. We also propose ART (articulate, retrieve, test), a staged paradigm that exposes each decision as an inspectable output. Extensive experiments with five model configurations show that systems fail mostly at choosing which records count, a verdict-evidence gap that accuracy alone conceals. ART closes most of this gap and brings a 31B open model to within 0.01 of the frontier models under the same paradigm; the frontier models succeed once given the codebook.

title: RoboAtom: Large-scale Atomic-Action Supervision for Robot Learning
abstract: Fine-grained action annotations can support skill reuse and compositional generalization in robot policies. However, robot datasets typically provide task-level instructions without subtask annotations. Although some include subtask labels, inconsistent formats and conventions hinder cross-source joint training. We propose RoboAtom-Data, which adds unified, time-aligned atomic-action annotations to existing data from multiple sources, covering 1.45 million trajectories, 6.88 million skill-labeled segments, and 16,882.1 hours. Our pipeline combines a unified protocol, large-scale manual annotation, propagation across repeated executions with the same ordered skill sequence, and multi-stage quality control. We evaluate the dataset through automatic atomic-action annotation and robot control. We construct RoboAtom-Bench to standardize evaluation of skill recognition and temporal boundary localization. Trained on the annotated data, RoboAtom-Anno achieves better automatic annotation performance than all evaluated open- and closed-source models on both RoboAtom-Bench and the external WGO-Bench. For robot control, atomic-action supervision paired with hierarchical execution improves task success over task-level baselines on LIBERO-Long, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin. We will release the data, benchmark, model, and construction pipeline to support further research on skill-level robot learning.

title: An ODE-based Sampler for Discrete Diffusion Models
abstract: The marginals of a continuous diffusion model can be reproduced by a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), known as the probability flow ODE, which provides a foundation for accelerated sampling and consistency distillation. In this paper we address the question whether an analogous formulation exists for discrete diffusion models and answer it affirmatively by introducing exponential residual flows (ERFs). Our framework augments the discrete state with a continuous residual variable for each token and position. These residuals evolve deterministically according to piecewise-defined ODEs whose vector fields depend on the current discrete state and the forward and backward rate matrices of the prescribed diffusion model. The discrete state changes whenever a residual reaches zero. We prove that this construction preserves the marginals of the original diffusion. We derive a practical discretization of our sampler and specialize it to masked and uniform diffusion. The deterministic trajectories of ERFs support consistency distillation and yield empirical improvements over previous approaches across a variety of benchmarks including code and text generation tasks.

title: Mind The Gap (MTG-AD): Dataset and Fine-grained Evaluation for End-to-End Inline Audio Descriptions
abstract: Audio descriptions (AD) are essential for making visual media accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) users. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a scalable solution for generating audio descriptions on-demand, their performance on ``inline'' audio descriptions -- which must fit within existing silences in a video -- remains under-explored, particularly for diverse user-generated content (UGC). We present a comprehensive investigation into MLLM-generated inline audio descriptions. First, we introduce MTG-AD, a professionally annotated dataset of 36 hours of videos, each averaging sim5 mins. and 8k+ descriptions in total, co-created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals to provide a high-quality benchmark for this task. Second, we propose MTG-AD-Eval, an evaluation framework based on audio description expert guidelines that provides fine-grained, reference-free actionable metrics for model improvement. Crucially, our framework evaluates the end-to-end task: it renders the generated scripts into audio tracks to assess their fit within the original video's natural silences, minimizing disruptive overlaps. Our analysis across frontier MLLMs reveals that while models accurately describe visual events and substantially reduce speech overlaps, gaps persist in narrative pacing and flow. Finally, we empirically validate that our automated and reference-free metrics correlate significantly with human quality ratings from sighted raters and 7 BLV participants, finding that while users narrowly prefer human-authored audio descriptions, they find MLLM-generated audio descriptions highly beneficial for comprehension. We provide actionable system design guidance and release MTG-AD at https://hf.co/datasets/google/mind-the-gap-inline-ad and MTG-AD-Eval at https://github.com/google/mtg-ad.

title: Difficulty Calibration Across Time for Membership Inference in Diffusion Models
abstract: Modern diffusion models are trained on massive datasets that often include copyrighted or private images. Membership inference attacks (MIAs) address this by testing whether a given image was in a model's training set. The standard approach scores an image by its reconstruction loss and flags low-loss images as members. This often fails because some images are simply easier to reconstruct than others, so a simple unseen image can score a lower loss than a complex training image. Difficulty calibration separates memorization from how difficult an image is to begin with. We show how to calibrate along two axes of time: training time and diffusion time. First, across training time, we introduce Reference-Model Calibration (RMC), which compares a fine-tuned model's loss against an earlier checkpoint. This cleanly isolates newly memorized data and gives near-perfect auditing, even without text captions. Since earlier checkpoints are not always available, we next present Temporal Self-Calibration (TSC), which calibrates across diffusion time using only a single model. Our key observation is that an image's difficulty persists across noise levels, whereas memorization is localized in time. By comparing the loss at a target timestep against neighboring timesteps from the same model, TSC attenuates image difficulty using the model's own trajectory. Empirically, our methods beat the state of the art by a wide margin, and unlike most existing attacks, generalize across different model parameterizations such as $x$-, $v$-, and $ε$-prediction models. Code is available at https://github.com/MichaelJoseph777/TSC.

title: PhysAg3D: Bridging 3D Generative and Agentic Models for High-Fidelity and Physically-Interactive Assets
abstract: Generating interactive 3D assets from a single image requires realistic appearance, fidelity to the depicted object, and plausible physical behavior. Yet detailed geometry alone does not determine how an object should move or deform. We introduce PhysAg3D, which couples 3D generative models with agentic reasoning and tool use. A vision-language agent first infers semantic parts, candidate interactions, and physical priors from the image; a 3D generator then produces a textured whole-object mesh from the same image. A hierarchical interaction representation links these revisable priors to mechanisms and the generated surfaces they control, organizing interaction construction and refinement. Guided by this representation and observations of the mesh, the agent uses geometric and physical tools to construct parts, joints, deformable regions, and surface bindings while retaining useful generated geometry and materials. Rendered interactions and execution measurements guide targeted revisions within a fixed budget. The framework accommodates both rigid articulation and compliant deformation. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations on real photographs and external benchmarks demonstrate detailed, image-aligned assets with plausible interactions. Ablations support bounded refinement and source-surface preservation. Project Page: supra-3d.github.io/PhysAg3D.
