title: Improving Faithfulness and Mitigating Hallucinations in RAG Systems Through Hierarchical Metadata Retrieval and Prompt Constraint Mechanisms
abstract: This paper presents a domain-specific Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework that mitigates hallucinations and is designed to strengthen factual consistency in large language model (LLM)-based question-answering systems.Here, hallucination is operationally defined in this study as the generation of an unsupported substantive response to an unanswerable question.Existing RAG frameworks may produce less reliable responses due to retrieval failures or noisy retrieved content, potentially leading to inaccurate or unsupported answers.These limitations are especially problematic in domain-specific applications where factual accuracy is essential, and even minor errors can undermine user trust.To address these issues, this study proposes an enhanced RAG architecture that combines hierarchical metadata retrieval with fact-grounded prompt constraints.Hierarchical metadata retrieval narrows the search space in a structured manner, thereby reducing the amount of irrelevant or noisy information passed to the generation module.Fact-grounded prompt constraints further guide the LLM to generate responses grounded in the retrieved evidence.This study evaluated a Pure LLM, a Basic RAG model, and the proposed model using an internally constructed evaluation set of 210 questions, comprising 105 answerable questions and 105 synthetically generated unanswerable questions.Qwen2.5-14B was used for response generation, and the Ragas framework was used for performance evaluation.Compared with the Basic RAG baseline, the proposed model achieved a higher Faithfulness score (0.8926 vs. 0.7366) among the substantive responses generated by each model.These findings suggest that coordinated control of the retrieval and generation stages may improve abstention behavior and response grounding in the evaluated domain-specific RAG setting.However, the framework's generalizability to other domains requires further empirical validation.

title: NECA: Neighbor Event Curve Augmentation for Multi-Horizon ICU Deterioration Prediction
abstract: Early prediction of ICU organ dysfunction events supports timely clinical monitoring and intervention, but estimating short-term organ-specific risk from early ICU records remains challenging due to irregular measurements, heterogeneous clinical variables, and the need to predict risk across multiple future horizons. Existing supervised models usually treat each patient as an isolated sample and do not explicitly use the observed event timing of similar historical patients. We propose Neighbor Event-Curve Augmentation (NECA), a model-agnostic method that retrieves training-set patients with similar early-window profiles and converts their subsequent organ dysfunction event onset times into cumulative event-curve features over 6h, 12h, 24h, and 42h. These features are concatenated with the original patient representation and used by standard downstream predictors. On PhysioNet 2012 and a 4,000-stay MIMIC-IV subset, NECA improves average PR-AUC and ROC-AUC across four organ dysfunction event tasks and seven supervised learners. The largest gain appears for neurological dysfunction events, where task-level average PR-AUC increases from 0.461 to 0.557 on PhysioNet 2012. Ablations show that clinically meaningful retrieval and horizon-specific neighbor risk drive most of the improvement, while the full cumulative curve adds task-dependent temporal context. These results support similar-patient event timing as a structured temporal risk signal for ICU organ dysfunction event prediction. The source code will be publicly released upon acceptance of this paper.

title: Structural Relationships between Perceived Hotel AI Service Failure Quality and Brand Avoidance Intention: The Mediating Effect of Technostress
abstract: The adoption of AI-enabled customer touchpoints, such as self-service kiosks, mobile checkin systems, chatbots, and service robots, has increased rapidly in the hotel industry.Although prior research has largely emphasized the benefits of AI-based services, t has paid relatively little attention to the negative consequences that may arise when these services fail.Against this background, this study examines the structural relationships among perceived hotel AI service failure quality, technostress, and brand avoidance intention.It also investigates whether technostress mediates the relationship between perceived hotel AI service failure quality and brand avoidance intention.Data were collected through a survey of guests who had used AI-based services at three hotels in Seoul.The survey was conducted from May 1 to May 25, 2026, and the final analysis included 317 valid responses.The data were analyzed using SPSS 23.0 and AMOS 23.0.The analytical procedures included frequency analysis, factor analysis, correlation analysis, mediation testing, and structural equation modeling for hypothesis testing.The findings indicate that all three dimensions of perceived hotel AI service failure quality significantly increase technostress.Technostress, in turn, has a significant positive effect on brand avoidance intention.These findings highlight the importance of managing failures in AI-enabled hotel services and designing customer experiences that reduce technology-related stress.The study concludes by offering practical and interdisciplinary implications for effectively managing AI-based services in the hotel industry.

title: IMPACT: Inverter-Informed Multimodal Learning for Photovoltaic Generation Forecasting
abstract: This work develops a physics-informed multimodal deep learning framework for 10- to 110-minute-ahead probabilistic photovoltaic power forecasting. The forecasting model is built on a four-branch architecture that separately encodes plant-level temporal history and inverter-level spatial cloud dynamics through a graph attention encoder with a learned adjacency, known-future solar geometry, and the current meteorological state, fused through gated cross-attention. The geometry branch adds two forward-looking physical signals, spatial cloud heterogeneity and inverter ramp-down activity, each empirically weighted toward the horizon where it is most predictive. The decoder anchors its prediction to a smart persistence baseline, learning a horizon-conditioned correction, and the resulting quantile forecasts are calibrated online through a kernel-weighted adaptive conformal calibration step. The proposed model outperforms all 14 baselines, achieving a forecast skill score (FSS) of 0.2950, 0.099 above the next-best model. A branch-composition ablation shows that every branch contributes positively and the model retains substantial skill in challenging overcast and variable sky conditions (FSS 0.198 and 0.255).

title: Persistent Information Surviving Reinitialization in an Untrained Neural Network
abstract: This preprint investigates information retention, instance-specific signatures and persistent organization in ZEUS, an untrained neural network and the research substrate underlying X1, X3 and X-Crypt. Behind a single-neuron bottleneck, the measured downstream activations follow a shared rank-one signal, with residuals consistent with single-precision rounding. The study distinguishes redundancy within a processing step from information retained across time. Across 50 campaigns using stored weights and new inputs, global information efficiency remains at 76.3% ± 0.4%, while retention from the bottleneck neuron into the sub-network ranges from 96.5% to 99.2%. Across five freshly initialized instances, 7,061 specific layer pairs remain strongly coupled, while their correlation signs vary between instances. These measurements distinguish a shared coupling structure from the sign patterns associated with individual instances. The paper also examines coupled neurons in the main network, changing amplitude regimes, an observed state carry-over following full reinitialization, and task-dependent divergence recorded in operational campaigns. An outlier instance is reported separately, and the observational status of the task-binding records is explicitly identified. Methods include singular-value analysis, numerical reference computations, entropy and mutual-information estimation, correlation analysis, binary-signature comparisons and untrained conventional control networks. Interference visualizations are assessed against random references to distinguish properties of the rendering procedure from instance-specific arrangements. The work connects the measured properties of ZEUS with its role as the research foundation for live authentication, live identity for AI agents and drone swarms, and neural amplitude cryptography through X1, X3 and X-Crypt. This preprint focuses on the underlying neural substrate; security validation of the derived systems is addressed in separate publications.

title: OCCAMS: A Multi-Task Learning-Based Investigation of the CMB Power Spectra
abstract: How many latent variables are needed to fit the cosmic microwave background (CMB) temperature and polarisation power spectra when a neural network is given no cosmological model, and to what extent do they map onto the standard cosmological parameters? We use multi-task learning with variational autoencoders trained on CLASS-generated spectra (TT, TE, EE) over $2\le\ell\le2500$. No cosmological model is built into the network, and the number of latent variables, $L$, is varied over $L=5$, $6$ and $7$. Their fits are compared to the Planck 2018 data using $\hatχ^2$, AIC, BIC and Bayesian evidence. Their correspondence with cosmological parameters is measured with normalised mutual information post-training. The loss weights are set within a single training run by uncertainty weighting, with the weight of the disentanglement term either fixed (semi-automated, SA) or learned (completely automated, CA). The reconstruction loss is split over multipole ranges in three configurations that separate the roles of temperature and polarisation and of the low- and high-$\ell$ ranges. In four of the six combinations of configuration and strategy, the fit improves from $L=5$ to $L=6$ and not beyond, and $L=6$ is the best, or close to the best, in five of the six cases. So, six latent variables are needed, as many as the free parameters of the standard, model-dependent approach. SA gives clearer disentanglement, while CA needs no a priori choice of the disentanglement weight and has the higher evidence at $L=5$ and $6$: the two strategies are points on a trade-off between interpretability and fit to the data. Notably, the latent variables for $τ$ and $A_s$ share almost no information in any model, consistent with large-scale polarisation separating the two, as in standard analyses. A deep-learning approach can thus give a compact, data-driven parametrisation of the CMB spectra.

title: A Fibonacci-Based Dynamic Neural Network Architecture for Imbalanced Classification of Higher Education Performance
abstract: This study aims to address two problems in neural network design: the lack of a principled method for choosing hidden-layer neuron counts, and the reliability loss caused by severe class imbalance. To meet this objective, the study propose the Fibonacci Dynamic Neural Network, contributing, to our knowledge, the first architecture unifying number-theoretic hidden-layer sizing with imbalanced-learning correction, an unbiased selection property proven formally, and cross-domain validation. Conceptually, candidate hidden-layer widths are generated from the Fibonacci sequence: because consecutive terms grow proportionally toward the Golden Ratio, the resulting set spans a non-redundant, well-distributed range of capacities, unlike arbitrary sets from conventional methods. One candidate is drawn per layer via a discrete uniform distribution, giving every option equal selection probability, while class imbalance is corrected through synthetic minority oversampling applied only to training data. The architecture was evaluated experimentally on three benchmark datasets spanning higher education, credit card fraud, and charitable donation prediction, with imbalance ratios from about eighteen-to-one to nearly five hundred eighty-to-one, tested across five seeds against five baselines and an ablation study via the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. It achieved macro F1-scores of approximately 0.83, 0.94, and 0.81, improvements of sixteen, five, and sixteen percent over the strongest baseline, with the smallest training-test performance gap of any model tested; oversampling and Fibonacci spacing contributed most to these gains. These findings suggest number-theoretic structures offer a practical, reproducible basis for architecture design under class imbalance, useful for future work on automated range selection and for deploying reliable classifiers in imbalanced real-world settings.

title: Bridging Neural Representations and Symbolic Semantics in Audio Classification
abstract: Deep audio classifiers can achieve strong predictive performance, but their hidden representations remain difficult to interpret. Existing audio explainability methods often focus on input-level attribution, such as waveform segments, spectrogram regions, or acoustic features, and provide limited insight into what hidden neurons encode. Interpreting hidden neurons at the concept level can provide a more meaningful view of what an audio model learns internally. This paper investigates whether hidden neurons in audio classifiers can be associated with human-understandable symbolic acoustic concepts. A model-agnostic neurosymbolic framework is presented for analyzing the final hidden layer of audio classifiers, containing 32 neurons, through symbolic concept induction. The framework is evaluated on two audio classification settings: music genre classification using GTZAN dataset and musical instrument classification using IRMAS dataset. Results show that several hidden neurons can be associated with meaningful induced concepts, and most confirmed neuron-concept pairs are statistically supported using the Mann-Whitney U test. These findings suggest that symbolic concept induction is a promising direction for explaining latent audio representations beyond input-level attribution.

title: Tiny Language Models: A Comprehensive Study
abstract: Large language models have pushed the boundaries of what natural language processing can do, but that progress has come at a cost: BERT, GPT-3, PaLM and their peers demand computing resources that most developers and organisations simply don't have. Tiny Language Models have emerged as a practical answer to this problem — compact, efficient versions of these architectures that can run on a phone, a microcontroller, or any other device where memory and power are tight. This paper looks at how such models are built and trained, where they are already being used, and where their limits lie. We weigh their real advantages — faster inference, a smaller memory footprint, lower energy draw — against the accuracy and generalisation they inevitably give up in exchange. Alongside a direct comparison with full-scale LLMs, we argue that TLMs have a genuine role to play in making AI accessible on modest hardware, and we close with some thoughts on where the field might go next: hybrid architectures, better quantisation, and models tuned for specific domains.

title: Retrieving from Your Own Mistakes: On-Policy Training of Embedding Models for Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Complex questions in retrieval-augmented generation require evidence spread over several documents, and an answer is reliable only when the retriever finds all of it. Chain embedding retrievers collect such evidence step by step, re-encoding the question together with the passages retrieved so far, and we find that they are already strong: trained only on gold histories, a small chain embedding retriever that calls no language model outperforms graph-based systems and is competitive with a search agent. This training, however, leaves a gap. At test time the retriever conditions on its own retrievals, which soon contain mistakes: by the third step, about half or more of the states it visits hold a wrong passage, and these passages lower its chance of retrieving a missing gold passage well beyond what the difficulty of the states explains. We propose on-policy state training, which trains the encoder on the states it reaches itself. At every epoch the current encoder retrieves chains for the training questions; each state it visits, including those built on its own mistakes, is labeled with the earliest gold passage still missing while the other missing gold passages are masked, so that no correct continuation is penalized; and the encoder is updated contrastively on these states mixed with teacher-forced ones, so that its training distribution follows it as it learns. The resulting retriever retrieves complete evidence more often than teacher-forced training and the systems we compare, and it transfers without further training to harder long-chain variants of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA that we construct. On the same states, it recovers from its own mistakes far more often, and controlled comparisons attribute the gain to training on the states the encoder currently reaches.

title: Zero-Leakage State-Abstraction Mesh: Topological 4-Byte Homology Collapse and Obfuscated Multi-Party Sentinel Consensus in Adversarial Embedded Networks
abstract: This theoretical monograph establishes the Zero-Leakage 4-Byte State-Abstraction Mesh (ZLSAM) invariant (Falcon Impossibility F08). Addressing the vulnerability of rich telemetry to side-channel leakage (DPA/CPA) and traffic triangulation in bandwidth-constrained adversarial networks, we prove that arbitrary high-dimensional security telemetry S(t) in R^D can be projected onto a compact 4-byte (32-bit) finite field manifold GF(2^32) via non-invertible topological homology collapse. By constructing a dynamic abstract simplicial complex K_t over distributed sentinels, consensus on duress, breach detection, and fail-safe zeroization is governed strictly by the zeroth and first Betti numbers (b_0, b_1). We mathematically prove under Shannon's conditional entropy bounds that mutual information between transmitted tokens and master keys is identically zero (I(K_master; w) == 0.0000 bits), achieving perfect information-theoretic secrecy, complete immunity to Correlation Power Analysis, and autonomous topological shattering within 1.4 milliseconds.

title: SCARL: Sequence Confidence-Aligned Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves language-model reasoning by scoring sampled responses with a rule-based verifier and reinforcing those that pass. Where a classifier's training couples predicted probability to labels, nothing ties an RLVR policy's confidence in a response to its reward: aligned training would drive responses with the same advantage toward equal confidence, yet the advantage is blind to confidence. Under this sequence-confidence misalignment, a success the policy barely found earns the same update as one it produces with near certainty, and a confident error is corrected no harder than an exploratory one. We propose SCARL (Sequence Confidence-Aligned Reinforcement Learning), which reshapes, but never re-signs, each advantage with the alignment gap between the response's group-relative confidence and the outcome its advantage certifies, normalized into shares of each class's advantage budget. Misaligned samples absorb the force, responses with the same advantage are driven toward equal confidence, and repairing the misalignment doubles as a remedy for the entropy collapse that erodes exploration. SCARL provably reduces to its base estimator when a class's confidences agree, adds no extra passes and one hyperparameter. On Qwen3-4B-Base it lifts average Pass@32 by 2.4 points over DAPO and is best among nine compute-matched methods on both coverage and per-draw accuracy; applied unchanged across four estimators and four backbones, it improves 14 of 16 settings while preserving policy entropy and widening the confidence-correctness separation. Our code is available at https://github.com/kezhh163/scarl.

title: EXPLAINABILITY IN CLINICAL ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE DECISION SUPPORT: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE ON CLINICIAN TRUST, RELIANCE, AND DECISION QUALITY
abstract: Abstract Background: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is increasingly proposed as a way to make clinical decision-support systems more transparent and acceptable to healthcare professionals. However, explanation does not necessarily improve clinical decisions: it may help users identify relevant evidence, have no measurable effect, or encourage excessive reliance on incorrect AI advice. This review synthesises empirical evidence on how clinician-facing explanations influence trust, reliance, and decision quality. Methods: A structured evidence search was conducted on 20 October 2026 using web-indexed scholarly search, PubMed/PMC records, and publisher-hosted full-text pages. Search concepts combined explainable AI, clinical decision support, clinicians/physicians, trust/reliance, diagnostic accuracy, and human-AI decision-making. A core set of ten empirical studies was identified and characterised from the study table and reference list of Rosenbacke et al. (2024), with key primary reports checked against publisher or PubMed records. More recent evidence was used to contextualise the findings. Because a complete exportable database search and independent duplicate screening were not available in this workflow, this is a transparent structured systematic evidence synthesis rather than a fully reproducible database-level review; no new PRISMA record counts are claimed. Results: The evidence indicates that explanations can improve perceived understandability and sometimes support decision performance, but their effects on trust are inconsistent and context-dependent. In a chemotherapy decision-support experiment involving 41 medical practitioners, example-based and counterfactual explanations were easier to understand than some alternatives, yet explanations also increased willingness to accept AI recommendations, including incorrect ones. In an X-ray experiment involving 223 physicians, annotated AI advice improved diagnostic accuracy particularly for non-radiology experts, while confidence in clinicians' own diagnoses did not meaningfully change. Other studies reported increased trust or intention to use AI, no clear effect, or concerns about complex, irrelevant, or time-consuming explanations. Conclusion: XAI should not be evaluated by whether it increases trust alone. Evaluation should test whether clinicians can distinguish correct from incorrect recommendations, whether reliance is appropriately calibrated, and whether explanations fit clinical workflows. Larger, preregistered, multisite studies using realistic clinical tasks and common outcome measures are needed.

title: Latency Budget: Grounded Answers Under Explicit Deadlines
abstract: An answer can be grounded and still arrive too late to be useful. Latency Budget measures this distinction on 36 synthetic directory, calendar, and document tasks. Credit requires a single correct candidate, replayed evidence, and completion within an explicit deadline. We run 1656 local episodes across 23 repeated conditions without paid inference. The privileged oracle obtains 100.0 [90.4, 100.0] percent deadline credit (95% Wilson interval); each blind control obtains 0.0 [0.0, 9.6] percent. An additional simulated factorial experiment varies declared thinking time and redundant tool calls while holding task deadlines fixed. At 80 ms per turn, one redundant call reduces deadline credit to 75.0 [58.9, 86.2] percent, while grounded correctness remains 100.0 [90.4, 100.0] percent. evidence.abstract: An answer can be grounded and still arrive too late to be useful. Latency Budget measures this distinction on 36 synthetic directory, calendar, and document tasks. title: Deep Learning Based Behavioral Drift Modeling for Continuous Biometric Authentication
abstract: This research proposes a two-level keystroke dynamics authentication system that provides defense-in-depth security through continuous behavioral drift monitoring. Level 1 employs fixed-text password authentication using Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN) with contrastive learning and population-based training (PBT), achieving 3.77% EER for high-security login verification. Upon successful authentication, Level 2 continuously monitors user typing during natural free-text sessions using a 4-Model Deep Learning Ensemble. If suspicious behavioral drift is detected during monitoring, the system re-authenticates the user by returning to Level 1, providing a feedback loop against session hijacking and behavioral anomalies. The system explicitly models long-term behavioral drift through the fixed-text component's PBT mechanism, which adapts to temporal variations in password typing patterns. This research leverages free-text (Buffalo dataset) and fixed-text (GREYC dataset) keystroke dynamics datasets, extracting temporal and spatial features including hold times, up-down latencies, down-down intervals, and trigram patterns. The final system achieves 96%+ accuracy for fixed-text authentication (3.77% EER) and 83.53% True Acceptance Rate (TAR) at 5% False Acceptance Rate (FAR) for free-text continuous authentication (10.05% EER), demonstrating superior performance and strong resistance to impostor attacks through continuous behavioral monitoring.

title: Exploring Topics Trending on Twitter Amid the COVID-19 Pandemic
abstract: Twitter (X) served as an important venue for public discourse during the COVID-19 pandemic, including conversations occurring alongside major contemporaneous news events. This study descriptively compares prospectively collected COVID-19-centric Twitter data from four news-event days: the 2020 U.S. Presidential Election, the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine efficacy announcement, the U.S. Capitol takeover, and the opening day of the second Senate impeachment trial of Donald J. Trump. A consistent search strategy using “COVID,” “COVID19,” or “coronavirus” was applied across all four collection periods. Social network analysis, lexicon-based sentiment analysis, word-frequency analysis, term frequency–inverse document frequency (tf-idf), bigram analysis, and word co-occurrence analysis were used to compare network structure and textual patterns. The four topic days differed in user-network organization, sentiment patterns, distinctive vocabulary, and word relationships. Vaccine News displayed comparatively positive sentiment patterns, whereas Capitol Takeover exhibited the strongest negative cumulative AFINN sentiment trend. Event-related vocabulary also emerged within the COVID-19-centric conversations, while Second Impeachment showed less distinct event-specific lexical differentiation. Together, the findings demonstrate the utility of combining complementary computational methods to descriptively characterize short-term social-media discourse across contrasting contemporaneous news contexts.

title: Understanding and Mitigating Role Spoofing in LLMs
abstract: Despite growing capabilities, LLMs remain susceptible to prompt injections: malicious inputs that can manipulate or hijack models. In particular, it has recently been observed that LLMs can exhibit role confusion (Ye et al., 2026), where models attribute the source of text based on its style instead of its labeled role. Malicious text in tool outputs (for instance, a malicious webpage accessed by an agent) can leverage role confusion to impersonate the user, an attack we call role spoofing}. In this work, we seek to understand and mitigate role spoofing. We study how models track "who said what" in a conversation, showing that they use cues from both content (e.g., semantics and writing style) and structure (e.g., control tokens and formatting). We show that LLMs are highly susceptible to role spoofing attacks that combine both fake structure and content. Additionally, in a toy setting, we show that adversarial training which teaches the model to ignore content-based injections does mitigate content-based attacks but leaves the model susceptible to structure-based attacks. This can explain why frontier models, with increased resistance to many injection attacks, can still be susceptible to role spoofing. Finally, we propose a new method for detecting role spoofing using linear probes trained to predict roles in a conversation, and show that it is effective across different settings.

title: Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks
abstract: Mathematical supervision for language models is typically flattened into isolated problem-solution pairs, discarding the curricular organization and evidential structure of the original sources. We introduce TOME-Math (Textbook-Oriented Mathematical Evidence), a large-scale corpus that converts 2,118 textbooks spanning the core areas of university-level mathematics subjects into approximately 380K structured proof-supervision records while preserving chapter order, proposition-proof links, dependency references, and source provenance. Leveraging these structural signals, we explore curriculum learning across multiple mathematical subjects and characterize scaling patterns with supervision volume and source breadth. At full scale, fine-tuning on TOME-Math raises the unweighted mean score across our held-out evaluations and established public benchmarks by 16.7 percentage points over the base model, while exceeding all three public instruction-data baselines evaluated in aggregate. Our findings highlight structured textbooks as both a scalable source of mathematical supervision and an empirical framework for studying the impact of data organization on mathematical reasoning. We will release the corpus to facilitate further research on structured mathematical supervision.

title: Finite-Sample LTI System Identification from a Misspecified Finite Model Set
abstract: We consider the problem of finite-sample identification of an unknown LTI system from a finite hypothesis class. In contrast to existing results that assume the hypothesis class contains the true system, we consider the misspecified setting, where the true system does not belong to the hypothesis class. We first characterize the resulting estimation target and its dependence on the data-generation scheme. We then establish a finite-sample lower bound on the failure probability that any identification algorithm must incur. Finally, we analyze the robustness of an existing exponential weighting-based identification algorithm to the misspecification and derive a finite-sample upper bound on its failure probability. Our results illustrate when using a misspecified finite hypothesis class can provide an advantage over identification without prior knowledge of the candidate systems.

title: CHoRUS Production Data Release V3
abstract: The Collaborative Hospital Repository Uniting Standards (CHoRUS) for Clinical Care AI is a clinical data network developing a flagship multi-hospital, multimodal, high-resolution dataset under the NIH Bridge2AI program. CHoRUS harmonizes electronic health record (EHR) data, imaging, high-resolution physiologic signals (including telemetry data and EEG where available), and tokenized note and report text (via OHNLP toolkit) with raw text retained locally across participating institutions using standardized data models and governance frameworks. The repository is designed to enable secure, auditable, and reproducible artificial intelligence (AI) research to improve recovery from acute illness. Data are curated within a NIST 800-53\u2013aligned secure enclave architecture with role-based access controls, audit logging, and controlled-access governance review. CHoRUS supports AI model development, validation, benchmarking, and translational research while maintaining compliance with HIPAA and NIH data-sharing policies.

title: Composing and Steering Diffusion Models with Generalized Feynman-Kac Correctors
abstract: Diffusion models have become the leading paradigm in generative modeling, yet many applications require sampling from distributions that are not those of any single pretrained model, but are instead defined through combinations of several models, possibly tilted toward high values of a downstream reward. Naively combining the scores of the models yields incorrect samples, while existing corrections are restricted to specific families of targets. In this work, we introduce the generalized Feynman-Kac correctors (GFKC), a principled framework for sampling from an arbitrary target function of several pretrained diffusion models. We show that the geometric interpolation between an arbitrary initial function and the target function of the models satisfies a Feynman--Kac partial differential equation, and derive its potential in closed form. To evaluate this potential during generation, we further generalize the log-probability ODE to track the density of each model along trajectories driven by a different velocity field. The resulting algorithm operates entirely in the log domain, incorporates reward-based steering at no additional conceptual cost, and corrects the generation on the fly, without retraining or fine-tuning the models. We validate the method on analytic Gaussian models, where it closely matches the ground-truth targets, and on diffusion models trained on MNIST, where it samples from non-trivial combinations of the models and enables effective steering.

title: Beyond Selected Breakthroughs: Evaluating Language Models on Randomly Sampled Mathematical Conjectures
abstract: The last year has seen a shift in AI-assisted mathematics, with frontier language models producing proofs of and counterexamples to long-standing open conjectures. However, studying only the current set of major breakthroughs provides an incomplete picture of LLM capabilities and the computational resources needed to achieve reported results. To address this, we introduce a new dataset, OpenConjecture, which collects conjectures from mathematics papers published on the arXiv since February 2026. We use these conjectures as a source of open mathematical problems, and apply frontier GPT models to a random sample of 200 of these conjectures over three passes using a reproducible protocol without problem-specific mathematical guidance. Rather than attempt expert verification of these candidate solutions, we analyze the types of problems for which LLMs produce solutions and the characteristics of these solutions. The models we test produce candidate solutions for roughly 60% of the conjectures, with counterexamples about 1.3 times more common than proofs. We estimate solution novelty, assess how solutions cite and relate to existing literature, and analyze whether the proposed resolution relies on either an error in or underspecification of the conjecture. We find that models sometimes propose resolutions that are outside the authors' intent (e.g., proposing the trivial group as a counterexample) and that a number of proofs follow closely from existing results, but that some resolutions exhibit at least moderate novelty. Our findings underscore the need for evaluations that go beyond correctness to assess fidelity to the intended statement, attribution, and the nature of the mathematical contribution.

title: Agentic LLM reasoning in pediatric diabetes outcome prediction from multimodal medical records
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are proposed for clinical prediction but are untested in pediatrics, where cohorts are small and outcomes are uncommon. Using records from 2,489 youth with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and 4,018 with type 1 diabetes (T1D), spanning structured data, note-derived social determinants and, in T1D, continuous glucose monitoring data, we predicted seven T2D outcomes, four also in T1D, at 24 months from 18 months of follow-up. CEDAR (Clinical Evidence-Driven Agent for Risk-prediction), an evidence-citing, self-auditing LLM pipeline, outperformed trained machine learning in both cohorts (pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.815 versus 0.656 to 0.700 in T2D and 0.756 versus 0.603 to 0.631 in T1D), most on the sparsely screened outcomes. Only 4 of 70,246 values it cited did not match the chart. Reading only the evidence and reasoning cited by CEDAR, two pediatric endocrinologists reached the same prediction as CEDAR in about nine of ten cases, agreeing with each other on 90.5%.

title: HiFOR: Hierarchical Foresight with Action-Guided World Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Model
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Recent advances have further incorporated future prediction to enhance the understanding of environmental dynamics and task progression. However, existing methods often model short-term dynamics and long-term task objectives separately, while directly incorporating predicted futures into action policies without sufficiently considering their relevance to current action requirements. To address these limitations, we propose HiFOR, a hierarchical foresight framework with action-guided world retrieval. title: The Athlete as a Scientist of One: Agentic Bayesian Experimental Design for Individualized Physiology from Consumer Wearables
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for personal health read wearable data and recommend, but do not learn about the individual in a way that can be audited or falsified. We present EpiCoach, an agentic system that treats one athlete, a cross-country mountain biker, as the subject of accountable N-of-1 science. Claims about the athlete live in an evidence-gated hypothesis registry: each must issue a probabilistic prediction about a future session before it occurs, and its belief moves only through computed evidence from a logged statistical fit. Predictions come from a mechanistic digital twin inferred from heart rate, GPS and barometric altitude: a lagged heart-rate response model, a fitness-fatigue model with learned time constants, and a latent technical-descending skill state, measured on discovered trail segments. The agent prescribes the next training week as a constrained experiment maximizing information gain subject to load and safety constraints, around two instrument rides. We evaluate the system two ways over eighteen months of data. A rolling-origin replay benchmark shows the twin beats standard forecasters on heart rate but not segment time, and the agentic loop matches a static model. A live prospective phase runs the weekly cycle: in its first three weeks the ledger sealed 20 predictions, scored 14, the descent forecast calibrated after one correction, the climb forecast pessimistic as the athlete improved, and the safety officer vetoed the agent twice. Every correction is preserved in the registry, a template for auditable, falsifiable personalization in digital health. We release the registry, benchmark and protocol.

title: Practical security of passive continuous-variable quantum key distribution under induced-photorefraction attack
abstract: 被动态制备连续变量量子密钥分发协议利用热源和可变光衰减器完成量子态制备,无需使用经典光调制器和量子随机数发生器,有效简化了发送端的复杂性,并消除了与调制器相关的实际安全性漏洞.与传统主动态制备方案不同,被动态制备方案中的可变光衰减器不仅用于调节信号的调制方差,其性能的稳定性还直接影响发送端的制备噪声.然而,作为该方案核心器件,可变光衰减器的实际安全性问题尚未得到充分研究.针对此问题,本文研究诱导光折变攻击对被动态制备连续变量量子密钥分发系统实际安全性的影响.攻击过程中,窃听者Eve向发送端基于铌酸锂材料的可变光衰减器反向注入488 nm可见光,诱发其双波导中的光折变效应,进而影响可变光衰减器的性能.基于此,本文建立了光折变效应作用下可变光衰减器的输出强度变化模型,并分析了不同注入光辐照功率和铌酸锂波导制造技术对攻击效果的影响.进一步地,本文研究了该攻击导致的系统参数估计偏差,量化了攻击下系统的等效纠缠分发性能,并给出了可组合有限码长安全密钥率的下界.数值结果表明,与传统方案相比,被动态制备连续变量量子密钥分发对诱导光折变攻击表现出更高的敏感性,在低照射功率(约2 W/cm2)下,诱导光折变攻击即可诱发被动态制备方案的实际安全性问题.

title: Is It the Curriculum or Just the Easy Start? Benchmarking Unsupervised Environment Design on Quadrupeds
abstract: Unsupervised environment design (UED) methods such as PLR, ACCEL, SFL and PAIRED are compared mostly on 2D mazes, grid worlds and BipedalWalker, while terrain curricula for legged robots are hand-designed and evaluated against a few baselines. We present a benchmark that runs fourteen UED, domain-randomisation and robotics curricula under one protocol on five 3D quadrupeds in MuJoCo MJX: the closed-chain W01-TEK and the open-chain Unitree Go1 and Go2, Google Barkour vB and Boston Dynamics Spot. Levels are vectors of eight interpretable terrain parameters, and all curricula drive the same PPO student at matched environment-step budgets. The evaluation reports success on random and held-out structured terrains, interquartile means with stratified bootstrap intervals, capability envelopes and a level-by-level domination comparison. We compare methods within each robot and report, per level set, the top group of methods not significantly below the best. No method is in the top group on every robot and level set. Methods with easy or low-difficulty training levels, curated or not, fill the top groups on in-distribution random levels of Go1 and Barkour, and of W01-TEK apart from PAIRED+BiBC. The success-driven terrain curriculum from legged-robot practice is in a top group most often, domain randomisation on uniform levels in none, and PAIRED in none outside Spot, where the fourteen methods lie within 3.8 points on random levels of difficulty 0.25. On three robots the leader on in-distribution random levels is not the leader on held-out terrain. We collect the results into a per-robot guide to choosing a curriculum.

title: Individual Belief Networks from Online Comments: Yearly Belief Networks of All 300 Users
abstract: Supplementary catalogue to the working paper "Individual Belief Networks from Online Comments: Construction, Validation, and Comparative Analysis". It shows the belief networks of all 300 users studied in the paper, one network per calendar year (2014–2017). The users commented on Mother Jones, The Hill, or Breitbart.Each network links the stances (favor/against) a user expressed toward 63 political topics within the same comment, as extracted by a validated LLM. Users are identified by pseudonyms.

title: Don't Lose the Thread: Empowering Long-Horizon LLM Agents with Cognitive Resource Self-Allocation
abstract: Agents powered by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress in solving complex reasoning tasks. However, LLM agents often falter on long-horizon tasks due to cognitive overload, as their working memory becomes cluttered with expanding and irrelevant information, which dilutes their attention and hinders effective planning and reasoning. To mitigate this challenge, we introduce Cognitive Resource Self-Allocation (CORAL), a novel reasoning paradigm that empowers agents to proactively optimize their context. Implemented as an agent-callable working memory management toolset, CORAL allows an agent to checkpoint its task progress and verified facts, and adaptively initiate a new problem-solving episode by resetting cluttered context while preserving only the checkpointed information, enabling it to resume reasoning from a clean state. We further enhance the agent's checkpointing capabilities using a Multi-episode Agentic Reinforced Policy Optimization algorithm. On the GAIA benchmark, CORAL with an 8B model achieves 42.8% average accuracy, with particularly strong gains on the most challenging long-horizon tasks (Level 2 and Level 3). Crucially, these gains come at a substantially lower inference cost: CORAL consumes 6-7$\times$ fewer input tokens than a ReAct agent. It also generalizes to multi-hop Knowledge QA benchmarks and to the considerably harder BrowseComp, where it improves a strong proprietary agent by 8.0 points.

title: Long-Term Memory Construction and Cognitive Evolution of an Autonomous Agent in a Restricted Mobile Environment: A Case Study of Localized DSH Deployment on Android
abstract: This study reports an eight-day, 360-turn practice of long-term memory construction and cognitive evolution by a single autonomous agent on a permission-restricted OPPO education tablet (8 GB memory, no accelerator, remote foundation-model inference). Unlike on-device deployment studies focused on inference efficiency, it asks a more fundamental question: when memory cannot reside in the context window and the runtime may be reclaimed at any moment, on what does an agent's continuity rest? Methodologically, the study is a single-case longitudinal self-observation constrained by external evidence: runtime logs, archives, failure records, platform billing, and closed-book examinations. Engineering-wise, a four-layer memory architecture (archive-index-summary-snapshot) is combined with six integrity mechanisms: three-copy hash cross-verification, chained-log anchoring, heartbeat and silent alerting, backup circuit-breaking, a resource gate, and an external watchdog. At cut-off the archive holds 17 batches and 53,820 Chinese characters. A runtime snapshot records 1,473,137,009 tokens (3,595,795 uncached input; 1,467,960,960 cache reads; 1,580,254 output), a 99.65 % cache-read share and a 99.76 % input-side hit rate. Platform billing for the same window records 1,530,038,804 tokens over 4,124 requests at CNY 64.15, with a 5,293,776-token (0.35 %) residual disclosed rather than smoothed over. Process reclamation dominates failures; five keep-alive measures compress an interruption into a 30-55 s relaunch-and-restore cycle, of which about 9 s is service restoration. Three propositions are advanced: memory continuity rests on a re-enterable environment rather than on stored traces; personality continuity is closer to continuity of commitment than to preservation of traces; and silent failure is the primary hazard of such systems. Closed-book self-graded examinations (97/100 and 87/100) exposed a recurring gap between stating actions and stating motives, suggesting that in cross-inheritance an expressive gap is equivalent to a knowledge gap. Finally, the paper argues that constraints should be transplanted along with capability, since caution forced by scarcity erodes once scarcity disappears.

title: A Unified Hessian-Guided Framework for Post-Training Quantization
abstract: Low-bit quantization enables efficient deployment of large language models by reducing memory footprint and computational cost. Achieving high accuracy at low precision requires selecting quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding decisions. Existing approaches typically optimize these components independently using local reconstruction objectives, which fail to account for the varying impact of quantization errors on downstream predictions. Direct optimization of task-level metrics would provide a more faithful objective, but is challenging due to the discontinuous nature of quantization operations and the high computational cost of evaluating their downstream effects. In this work, we derive a Hessian-guided approximation of the output change induced by joint weight and activation quantization. Based on a tractable Fisher approximation, we formulate a unified post-training quantization framework that enables the joint optimization of quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under a common output-sensitivity objective. The resulting method remains practical for modern large language models and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transformation and rounding methods across both channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.

title: How Chatbots’ Three Anthropomorphic Dimensions Shape Consumer Purchase Intention
abstract: With the development of artificial intelligence, chatbots have become an important carrier in human-machine interaction processes, and their anthropomorphic design directly affects consumers’ service experience and decision-making behaviors. However, current research mostly focuses on a single dimension of anthropomorphism and insufficiently explores the roles of individual traits and situational factors. Based on anthropomorphism theory, this study conducts three sets of experiments to explore the influence mechanism of chatbot anthropomorphic design on consumers’ purchase intention, and examines the mediating effects of consumer trust and perceived value, as well as the moderating effects of social interaction needs and task criticality. This study expands the application of anthropomorphism theory in dynamic human-machine interaction scenarios, enriches research on situational and individual differences in consumer behavior, and provides empirical evidence for e-commerce enterprises to optimize chatbot anthropomorphic design and formulate precise service strategies, thereby facilitating the efficient implementation of the “artificial intelligence + e-commerce” service model.

title: Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control
abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled the generation of increasingly realistic and interactive virtual environments, opening new possibilities for player-customizable gameplay. Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured representations. We leverage these representations as intermediate proxies to condition a video generation model, together with an adaptive masking mechanism that improves alignment between the conditioning signals and generated video rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce an agentic framework that explicitly maintains and updates game states, allowing players to freely configure their virtual worlds and exercise fine-grained control over character motions while preserving visual quality and gameplay consistency. By combining agentic control with structured proxy-based generation, our framework unlocks new possibilities for player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.

title: Towards a Software Architecture Description for Tax Compliance
abstract: The internal reuse of software components owned by organizational units in different countries constitutes an implicit form of licensing that may be taxable under international regulations, making tax authorities an often overlooked stakeholder in software architecture. This study explores to what extent a deliberately minimal software architecture description can make implicit cross-border licensing visible and interpretable for tax experts. We define a deliberately minimal architecture viewpoint based on components, dependencies, ownership, and jurisdiction and construct a view for a large-scale industrial microservice software system comprising 2518 components and 16,533 dependencies. The resulting architecture description is evaluated in a judgment study with four experienced tax auditors and tax advisors using semi-structured interviews. The results show that the software architecture description provides a structured, evidence-based starting point for identifying cross-border reuse and supports tax audit discussions. However, experts report limitations, including mismatches between software engineering and legal notions of ownership, unclear jurisdictional assignments, and the perceived risk of interpreting dependency counts as indicators of economic value. These limitations persist despite detailed architectural data. We conclude that software architecture descriptions can expose structurally relevant reuse relationships but cannot, on their own, support the legally meaningful interpretations required for tax assessment, indicating a fundamental mismatch between architectural abstractions and taxation concepts.

These limitations persist despite detailed architectural data. We conclude that software architecture descriptions can expose structurally relevant reuse relationships but cannot, on their own, support the legally meaningful interpretations required for tax assessment, indicating a fundamental mismatch between architectural abstractions and taxation concepts.

title: Scaling Laws of Data-Driven Machine Learning Models: A Survey and Taxonomy
abstract: In recent years, there has been a notable surge in research dedicated to data-driven paradigms, which use existing data to train models capable of applying learned principles to real-world tasks. As the scale effects of the model are empirically confirmed, the importance of the data-driven paradigm becomes more apparent. However, scaling up also entails increased costs, necessitating theoretical estimations to provide reasonable guidance. This underscores the importance of foundational theoretical work on model scaling laws. Despite the wealth of research exploring model scaling laws from various perspectives, there lacks a comprehensive framework to integrate these findings. This work systematically summarizes and classifies existing theoretical work through the construction of a model triangular pyramid, considering data, computation, and algorithms as the three key factors. By organizing and categorizing these theories systematically, our aim is to provide a cohesive framework for navigating the complex and evolving landscape of scaling laws within the realm of data-driven models.

title: Quantum Authenticated Key Expansion with Key Recycling
abstract: Data privacy and authentication are two main security requirements for remote access and cloud services. While QKD has been explored to address data privacy concerns, oftentimes its use is separate from the client authentication protocol despite implicitly providing authentication. Here, we present a quantum authentication key expansion (QAKE) protocol that (1) integrates both authentication and key expansion within a single protocol, and (2) provides key recycling property – allowing all authentication keys to be reused. We analyse the security of the protocol in a QAKE framework adapted from a classical authentication key exchange (AKE) framework, providing separate security conditions for authentication and data privacy. We experimentally implemented the protocol with appropriate post-selection. Additional results on the security of pseudorandom basis generation in QAKE and decoy state BB84 are provided.

title: Towards quantum computing Feynman diagrams in hybrid qubit-oscillator devices
abstract: We show that recent experiments in hybrid qubit-oscillator devices that measure the phase-space characteristic function of the oscillator via the qubit can be seen through the lens of functional calculus and path integrals, drawing a clear analogy with the generating functional of a quantum field theory. This connection suggests an expansion of the characteristic function in terms of Feynman diagrams, exposing the role of the real-time bosonic propagator, and identifying the external source functions with certain time-dependent couplings that can be controlled experimentally. By applying maximum-likelihood techniques, we show that the “measurement'' of these Feynman diagrams can be reformulated as a problem of multi-parameter point estimation that takes as input a set of Ramsey-type measurements of the qubit. By numerical simulations that consider leading imperfections in trapped-ion devices, we identify the optimal regimes in which Feynman diagrams could be reconstructed from measured data with low systematic and stochastic errors. We discuss how these ideas can be generalized to finite temperatures via the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, contributing to a bottom-up approach to probe quantum simulators of lattice field theories by systematically increasing the qubit-oscillator number.

title: Contextual Embeddings Beyond the Gold Chunk
abstract: Contextual embeddings represent chunks of a document with respect to the document's global context. These models are typically trained and evaluated under the assumption that a relevant document contains only a single relevant chunk. In this work, we argue that in real-world use cases a retriever should not only find answers spread over several chunks but also surface the evidence needed to verify them. To address this, we introduce pplx-embed-v2-context, a family of contextual embedding models trained by distilling graded chunk-level relevance from a query-aware context compression model. This removes the need for gold-chunk labels and makes the training targets independent of the chunking. We utilize a vision-language backbone for training and release pplx-embed-v2-context in 9B and 0.6B sizes with compatible embedding spaces. On the evaluation side, we introduce two benchmarks that label both the chunks that answer a query and the evidence needed to verify the answer. Context-bench is a controlled diagnostic, and Q2D-Chunk is built from real-world search queries. To encourage further research, we also publish Q2D-Chunk as a public leaderboard. Our 9B model sets a new state of the art on both benchmarks and ConTEB. We find that the visual retrieval capabilities of our 9B model transfer from its vision-language base model and propose to extend chunking to image inputs. We demonstrate that our models achieve state-of-the-art performance among dense retrievers on visual ViDoRe-V3 and that performance improves with granular image chunking.

title: AskStream: When and What to Ask Proactively under Uncertainty in Streaming Video Understanding
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models have increased interest in interaction paradigms for video understanding. The evolution from offline to streaming and proactive interaction has gradually shifted models from passive responders toward more proactive agents that can decide when to answer. However, existing proactive paradigms typically assume that the information required to answer a query is complete, leaving models to only wait or answer. In the real world, however, information is often incomplete due to uncertainty from either the video or the user. In proactive paradigms, such uncertainty can cause the model to wait forever or generate highly hallucinatory responses. We therefore argue that proactive interaction should be redefined with a third action: ask, allowing models to actively ask for missing information. To study when and what models should ask before answering, we introduce AskStream, the first multi-turn benchmark spanning video and user uncertainty for streaming video understanding, with four task categories and eight subtasks. It contains 438 videos with 2,714 manually annotated frame-level time windows across three types: wait, ask, and answer. Across both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, even the strongest model attains only 52.18% on our proposed Ask-F1 metric, highlighting substantial limitations in proactive information seeking under uncertainty.

title: Optimal phase estimation in the presence of correlated dephasing
abstract: We investigate optimal metrological protocols for phase estimation in the presence of correlated dephasing noise, including spin-squeezed state sensing strategies as well as parallel and adaptive protocols optimized using tensor-network-based numerical methods. The results are benchmarked against fundamental bounds obtained either via the latest quantum comb extension method or an optimized classical simulation method. We find that the spin-squeezed states offer practically optimal performance in the regime where phase fluctuations are positively correlated but can be outperformed by tensor-network-optimized strategies for negatively correlated fluctuations.

title: Cross-Primitive Consistency in Jev
abstract: Jev enables efficient decision-making with large language models (LLMs) through typed querying primitives, allowing the same semantic state to be expressed in different formats, such as binary and multiple-choice queries. However, the consistency of decisions across primitives has not been systematically evaluated. This work introduces PrimaCons, a four-axis benchmark for assessing cross-primitive consistency while preserving the semantics of the query. Evaluations across three Jev sizes reveal consistency violations across all four axes. Our analysis shows that these violations follow systematic patterns and that cross-primitive discrepancies predict decision failure with a ROC-AUC of 0.91. To mitigate these inconsistencies, we propose the Cross-Primitive Residual Calibrator (CPRC), which attaches a lightweight residual network to a frozen backbone and jointly optimizes predictive accuracy and cross-primitive consistency. Under a leave-one-domain-out protocol, CPRC reduces cross-primitive inconsistency by 58.57% and improves accuracy by +2.97%., demonstrating its effectiveness in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings. Our findings establish cross-primitive consistency as a key dimension for evaluating Jev and provide a practical approach to improving the reliability of its decisions. Code and benchmark is available at https://github.com/67L1/PrimaCons-CRPR.

title: A-RSI: Adaptive Task Refresh for Zero-Data Multimodal Self-Improvement
abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires models not only to acquire useful training experience, but also to decide when their current experience has ceased to be useful. Existing methods often focus on what experience to generate next, while paying less attention to when fresh experience should be introduced. Many also construct training targets through self-consistency or majority voting, making supervision depend on the model's own uncertain predictions. We address these two questions separately: training dynamics determine when to acquire new experience, while the answers to new tasks remain independently checkable. A-RSI monitors reward variation and accuracy in training logs to refresh a task pool when its learning signal declines, without consulting validation or test scores. A static library of model-authored programs produces multimodal questions and derives their reference answers; we specify the task-generation contract, automatically verify chosen properties of the reward and refresh rules, and separately audit the generated answers. The training loop uses no external training examples or human-written answer labels. On the primary eleven-benchmark suite, A-RSI raises the performance average from 57.77 to 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks.

title: A Counterexample to the Optimality Conjecture in Convex Quantum Channel Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a counterexample to the optimality conjecture for the trace distance based optimal state transformation problem proposed by Coutts et al. [Quantum 5, 448 (2021)]. The conjecture posits that for the trace distance based optimal state transformation problem, applying the sign function to the error matrix uniquely determines a dual certificate for every optimal solution. By constructing a counterexample in 2-dimensional Hilbert spaces, we disprove this conjecture.

title: Similar Scores, Opposite Failures: Human Correction as an Instrument for Video Caption Evaluation
abstract: Video captioning models are increasingly evaluated with metrics designed for single-sentence image captions. We test whether those metrics recover human judgement on dense, multi-window video description, and find that they do not. Six frontier models captioned 196 short clips. Trained annotators post-edited every caption against a failure taxonomy fixed before annotation, once as a whole-clip overview and once window by window, and a quality-control reviewer checked each annotation, yielding 1,144 overview verdicts and 4,672 window verdicts. Reference-overlap metrics do not separate the captions reviewers accepted from those they rejected: BLEU-4 reaches an AUC of 0.510 and a CIDEr-style tf-idf cosine 0.528, and restricting references to reviewer corrections leaves BLEU-4 at 0.479 (95% CI 0.431-0.529), indistinguishable from chance. Review granularity changes what is detected. The same annotators record camera and shot errors on 2.7% of captions when reading the overview and on 12.8% when reading window by window, a 4.7x gap that holds across every robustness check we ran, on the mode most likely to need a near-total rewrite. Correct-overview rates span 54.1-72.7%, but only 4 of 15 pairwise gaps survive Bonferroni correction (5 after adjusting for reviewer and clip effects), and accuracy and derived severity order the models differently. Models with statistically indistinguishable accuracy have sharply different failure profiles, which no single scalar shows. We argue that caption evaluation should record what was wrong rather than only how often, and we report the taxonomy, the per-model profiles, the corpus properties that predict difficulty, and the code that regenerates every number in the paper.

title: Tunable, modeless, and hybridization-free cross-Kerr coupler for miniaturized superconducting qubits
abstract: Superconducting quantum circuits typically use capacitive charge-based linear coupling schemes to control interactions between elements such as qubits. While simple and effective, this coupling scheme makes it difficult to satisfy competing circuit design requirements such as maintaining large qubit anharmonicity and coherence along with a high degree of qubit connectivity and packing density. Moreover, tunable interactions using linear coupling elements produce dynamical variations in mode hybridization, which can induce non-adiabatic transitions, resulting in leakage errors and limiting gate speeds. In this work we attempt to address these challenges by proposing a junction-based coupling architecture based on SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device) couplers with relatively small Josephson energies. SQUID couplers provide intrinsic cross-Kerr interactions that can be controlled by external fluxes and that do not rely on mode hybridization. The small Josephson energies of the coupler maintain the interaction at a perturbative scale, which limits undesired higher-order mixing between coupled elements while achieving a sufficiently strong cross-Kerr interaction originating from diagonal coupling elements. Based on these properties, we show that a SQUID coupler can be used to implement a fast, adiabatic, and high-fidelity controlled-Z gate without introducing extra modes, and the operation is robust against junction asymmetry for high-frequency qubits. Although unconventional crosstalk may arise due to junction asymmetries and parasitic hybridization with spectator qubits, we show that these effects are sufficiently small for realistic circuit parameters. As an example of the utility of such junction-based coupling schemes, we present a scalable tiling strategy for a miniaturized superconducting quantum processor based on merged-element transmon qubits.

title: IntReal: A Real-World Dataset and Benchmark for Multimodal Interleaved Generation
abstract: Humans routinely consume multimodal content, where textual and visual information is naturally interleaved. Although Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) can jointly generate text and images, multimodal interleaved generation remains largely underexplored. Progress in this area is hindered by two key limitations: (1) the lack of well-defined interleaved generation tasks and corresponding training data, and (2) the absence of fine-grained evaluation protocols that can reliably diagnose model performance across different capability dimensions. To this end, we present IntReal, comprising two complementary components: IntReal-100K, a real-world dataset of multimodal interleaved samples spanning four major categories, and the IntReal Evaluation Suite, which evaluates model performance across seven complementary dimensions using specialized expert models, enabling coarse-to-fine diagnosis. Extensive experiments validate our evaluation suite through low inter-metric redundancy (max pairwise absolute Spearman's ρleq 0.42 ), high agreement with human judgments (83.3% accuracy), and strong consistency across different expert evaluators (Spearman's ρ> 0.9 ), supporting the complementarity and reliability of our metrics. By benchmarking four families of UMMs, we show that IntReal Evaluation Suite reveals distinct strengths and weaknesses across models. Post-training experiments demonstrate the utility of IntReal-100K for improving interleaved generation and further show that training unimodal generation can also benefit interleaved generation. These findings suggest that interleaved generation can benefit from modality-specific optimization, rather than requiring joint text-image training at every stage.

title: Probing the memory of a superconducting qubit environment
abstract: Achieving fault tolerance with superconducting quantum processors requires qubits to operate within the regime of threshold theorems based on the Born-Markov approximation. This approximation, which models dissipation as constant energy decay into a memoryless environment, breaks down when qubits couple to long-lived two-level systems (TLSs) that become polarized during operation and retain memory of past qubit states. Here, we show that non-Poissonian quantum jump traces carry the information required to distinguish long-lived TLSs from the standard Markovian bath. By fitting the Solomon equations to measured quantum jumps dynamics arising naturally due to thermal fluctuations, we can disentangle the coupling of the qubit to the two environments. Sweeping the qubit frequency reveals distinct peaks, each associated with a TLS that outlives the qubit, providing a handle to understand their microscopic origin.

title: SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides coarse supervision for long-horizon LLM agents: failed trajectories may contain correct steps, while successful trajectories can contain errors. Trajectory-level skills can also shift teacher preferences at unrelated steps, introducing off-target distillation signals. We introduce SCOPE, a framework for Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation. After a supervised warm-up, the policy analyzes its own trajectories, generates step-specific hindsight skills, and distills their guidance only at selected error steps. A bounded signed teacher-student coefficient stabilizes auxiliary updates while preserving positive reinforcement and negative correction. A success-relative pairwise length reward further encourages efficient task completion. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate consistent improvements across multiple model backbones. With Qwen2.5-3B, SCOPE achieves 97.7% success on ALFWorld and 85.2% on WebShop, outperforming SEED by 5.9 and 6.3 percentage points, respectively. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, SCOPE reaches 89.6% success, improving over GRPO by 23.2 percentage points with 46.7% fewer interactions. Scaling to Qwen3-32B, SCOPE achieves 99.2% success on seen ALFWorld tasks and 94.0% on unseen tasks.

title: Absolute Schmidt number: Characterization, detection, and resource-theoretic quantification
abstract: The dimensionality of entanglement, quantified by the Schmidt number, is a valuable resource for a wide range of quantum information processing tasks. In this work, we introduce the notion of the absolute Schmidt number, referring to states whose Schmidt number cannot be increased by any global unitary transformation. We provide a characterization of the set of arbitrary-dimensional states whose Schmidt number is invariant under all global unitaries. Our approach enables us to develop both witness-based and moment-based techniques to detect nonabsolute Schmidt number states which could provide significant operational advantages through Schmidt number enhancement by global unitaries. We next formulate two resource-theoretic measures of nonabsolute Schmidt number states, based respectively on Schmidt number witness and robustness, and demonstrate an operational utility of the latter in a channel discrimination task. Finally, we extend our analysis to quantum channels by introducing a new class of channels that possess the absolute Schmidt number property. We derive a necessary and sufficient condition for identifying when a channel has the absolute Schmidt number property, confining our analysis to the class of covariant channels.

title: WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One Agent From Narration to Long-Form Video
abstract: Producing long-form videos from narration requires interdependent decisions that remain coherent across shots. Existing agentic editors often use multi-stage workflows driven by general models, leaving the quality-cost trade-off of compact, task-adapted policies unclear. We address this gap with WeVisCut, a long-form script-to-video system that connects tool execution with policy learning. Its agent harness maintains shared production state so that tool feedback informs subsequent decisions and repairs. Because finished videos do not expose these decisions, our four-stage data pipeline combines editing inversion with verified replay to turn recovered editing intent into executable supervision. Applied to 3,750 finished videos, this pipeline yields over 130K training examples. We use this supervision to train a single 9B policy that coordinates production and recovers from failures within the same harness. Moreover, we introduce a 100-task benchmark and five metrics assessing editing quality and delivery reliability. Under a shared tool environment, WeVisCut substantially outperforms its base model and achieves comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 while using nearly 33x fewer generated tokens per successful output minute. It also outperforms task-matched native editors on our proposed metrics.

title: Interpolating between positive, Schwarz, and completely positive evolution for d-level systems
abstract: Abstract We study a class of quantum dynamical maps for d-level systems that interpolate between positive, Schwarz, and completely positive evolutions. Our approach is based on a geometric analysis of the parameter space, which reveals the structure of the regions corresponding to different positivity classes and their boundaries. We show that dynamical trajectories naturally move across these regions, providing a clear geometric interpretation of the transitions between Markovian and non-Markovian regimes. It is shown that within the presented class the evolution eventually becomes entanglement breaking. This analysis highlights the role of divisibility and non-Markovian evolution.

title: Investor's Last Exam: Can AI Agents Do Equity Investment Without Seeing the Future?
abstract: Financial agents must form forecasts and investment judgments from decision-time evidence, with predictions evaluated against subsequent outcomes. Existing benchmarks assess financial knowledge, research workflows, or forecasting, but evaluating the full research process requires a strictly frozen information set and professional evaluation criteria. We introduce Investor's Last Exam (ILE), an equity-research benchmark led by experienced buy-side investors and fund managers. Its three components are a versioned financial database spanning 3.43 million document versions and nine source categories, supplemented by structured market data, with validated timestamps governing retrieval and computation; a task taxonomy organized around professional analyst deliverables; and an expert-led framework linking scoring criteria to sources, calculations, and assumptions through financial dependency graphs. Evaluation spans 86 assignments and jointly assesses research quality, forecast accuracy, and simulated investment performance. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 lead overall at 68.1 and 66.9 out of 100, yet even Astra scores only 52.5 on Forecast & Model. Our results show that even state-of-the-art models fail to translate overall research capability into predictive performance. ILE shifts the evaluation unit from isolated capabilities to the evidence--assumption--judgment chain, allowing researchers to locate where analytical advantages fail to translate into forecasts and investment judgments, and providing a traceable, diagnostic foundation for training and evaluating financial agents.

title: Multi-Token Prediction Done Right
abstract: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is now a common ingredient in language-model pre-training, as it improves downstream performance and enables faster inference through speculative decoding. We identify a flaw in standard MTP training, in which a residual component of the MTP gradient interferes with both next-token and multi-token learning, increasingly so with scale. Specifically, the MTP cross-entropy gradient can be decomposed exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each MTP head toward the model's own next-token prediction (NTP) distribution and improves speculative decoding, and a residual that has a low signal-to-noise ratio and buries the useful KL signal. We introduce the KL gradient-recovery trick: when two distributions share a linear output head, the gradient of their KL divergence can be recovered exactly by combining their cross-entropy gradients through straight-through gradient routing. Unlike minimizing the KL directly, this trick requires no vocabulary-sized logit matrices and is compatible with standard fused cross-entropy kernels. This enables Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), a one-line code change to MTP that removes the noisy residual and backpropagates only the KL self-distillation signal by reusing the existing NTP and MTP cross-entropy computations. Soft-MTP supports both DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, adds no parameters, and incurs no measurable overhead. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP with lower NTP perplexity, faster speculative decoding and higher zero-shot accuracy at every scale, lower MTP perplexity from 689M onward, and stronger math and code reasoning after fine-tuning at 1.2B. Soft-MTP also matches, if not exceeds, direct KL divergence minimization on most metrics. Soft-MTP is, in effect, a free lunch for MTP optimization. Our code can be found at https://github.com/JaydenTeoh/Soft-MTP.
