title: Quantum-enhanced estimation of stimulated Raman optical activity
abstract: In recent times there has been growing interest in Raman optical activity (ROA) for its label free detection of absolute configuration, conformation, and stereochemical structure in chiral biosamples and drug molecules. Since ROA signals are generally small, techniques such as stimulation by a probe beam can be used to enhance the signal strength. However, with a classical probe, the measurement precision is still fundamentally limited by its shot noise. To solve this problem we propose the use of two-mode squeezed vacuum and show that it can achieve sub-shot noise limited measurement sensitivity. Using quantum estimation theory, we derived the quantum Fisher information and the quantum Cramér-Rao bound (QCRB) for stimulated ROA measurement to quantify the precision enhancement. This improvement comes from photon-number correlations which suppress the intensity fluctuation common to both modes. We further show that balanced detection of the output intensity difference is a practical measurement scheme that approaches the QCRB and becomes optimal in the small-chirality limit. This opens a promising path toward more sensitive Raman chiroptical spectroscopy of weak and photosensitive samples.

title: Practical QCA-inspired quantum encryption with BB84 key distribution for NISQ devices
abstract: Reference implementation and reproducibility materials for the manuscript "Practical QCA-Inspired Quantum Encryption with BB84 Key Distribution for NISQ Devices" (Soumya S and T. Chithralekha, Department of Computer Science, Pondicherry University). The deposit contains the protocol implementation (BB84 key layer, QCA-inspired encryption/decryption, and the tag-based integrity-verification mechanism), the controlled-depolarising and backend-calibrated noise models, and a single reproducibility notebook that regenerates every table and figure in the manuscript from a fixed random seed (SEED = 42). No external datasets are used; all reported quantities are generated by simulation.

title: DecompGym: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Designing Decomposition Algorithms
abstract: Benders decomposition and column generation solve large optimization problems by passing cuts, columns, and dual values between a master problem and subproblems, and are hard to implement correctly. Large language models now automate parts of algorithm design, which points toward agents that build decomposition solvers for new problems. As a first step toward such agents, we study how well current coding agents design and implement these two algorithms, and how they fail. We introduce DecompGym, 81 instances from nine problem families (five Benders, four column generation), in which an agent writes a solver for a prescribed method. Each solver must meet three criteria: execution within a 60-second time limit; numerical feasibility together with a method audit, in which an LLM judge reads the solver's code; and an objective within 1% of the stored optimal objective. We evaluate 12 GPT, Claude, and Gemini models running in coding-agent tools. Over up to ten attempts, we compare independent regeneration with reflection, which first diagnoses the failure. On the first attempt, two models solve every instance and seven solve more than 90%. Most Benders failures (48 of 62) are missing or suboptimal solutions. The most common column-generation failure is a method-audit rejection. Output checks alone would accept 93 of the 108 attempts that fail the method audit. The most common rejection, an optimalif, occurs 96 times, 92 of them in one model.Reflection turns 66% of retries into successes, compared with 39% for regeneration, and it repairs method-audit failures, for which the judge names the defecective gaps. Agents for decomposition therefore need checks on how a solver reaches its answer and feedback that locates the error. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/SIKAI-C/DecompGym.

title: Scaling Lean Theorem Proving for Real-World Code Verification
abstract: We present EasyProver, a Lean proving system built from recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search, parallel tactic probing, and an elastic elaboration service. Using an off-the-shelf frontier model with no additional training, it proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations and resolves 597/600 NTP4VC verification conditions and all 189 VERINA tasks by proof or refutation. Because these benchmarks are close to saturation, we also introduce Aegis, which converts competitive programming problems into much harder verification tasks over real implementations. The pipeline writes safe Rust solutions, translates them into Lean with Aeneas, generates specifications, and labels each frozen statement with a kernel-checked proof or refutation. It produces 2,045 differentially validated Rust-Lean program pairs and 11,533 candidate specifications. Unlike hand-written benchmarks, these tasks carry implementation-level obligations from fixed-width arithmetic, explicit failure, generated loops, casts, and functionalized mutation. On a stratified sample of 2,000 statements, EasyProver proves 1,054 (52.7%) within a 30-minute budget per statement. The same tasks can also be used to benchmark other provers and as rewards for reinforcement learning.

title: Construction of a Class of Communication-Efficient Quantum Secret Sharing Schemes
abstract: Quantum secret sharing is a fundamental technique in quantum cryptography. However, in practical quantum networks, it still faces several bottlenecks, such as high quantum communication cost and low transmission efficiency. To reduce the communication cost, ramp quantum secret sharing schemes have been proposed in existing studies. Nevertheless, intermediate sets in such schemes may leak partial information about the secret. To address this problem, we develop a sufficient linear-algebraic criterion for such leakage, via a reduced channel and a secret-reference mutual-information witness; for ECSS, an explicit condition follows from a Vandermonde-type LU decomposition. We then propose a perfect-secrecy lifting of that communication-efficient ECSS construction, agnostic to the leakage form: the data-reconstruction structure and its d-participant cost are retained, while leakage is removed by a hybrid classical key layer. The information-theoretic secrecy statement is proved for the stated pre-announced reconstruction-set model. The channel-disturbance checks are treated as implementation-level auxiliary safeguards, not as part of the secrecy proof. The distribution-phase saving is model-dependent, whereas the data-reconstruction saving is not. We report intrinsic quantum communication, classical key-sharing, and storage resources under a common accounting convention, while auxiliary channel-checking overhead is reported separately for the proposed implementation.

title: brfssdata: Access CDC Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System Data
abstract: Download, cache, and analyze annual microdata from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS). Each requested survey year is downloaded once as a compact file hosted on public releases, verified against a published checksum, and cached locally; queries then run through DuckDB, so column selection and repeat analyses never re-transfer data. Survey-design helpers construct srvyr design objects with year-appropriate weights, strata, and primary sampling units, including explicit handling of the 2011 weighting methodology change and of the codes CDC uses for missing-type answers.

title: DICF: Domain-Invariant Counterfactual Explanations
abstract: One desired property of counterfactual explanations is plausibility, that is, a resemblance to real-world data. This property can be achieved by constraining counterfactuals lying in the data manifold. Unfortunately, the data often comes from multiple distinct environments (or domains) or changes under distribution shifts. This may alter the counterfactual validity and plausibility. To address this issue, we propose Domain-Invariant Counterfactual Explanations (DICF), a novel self-explaining framework rooted in invariant representation learning. By explicitly disentangling the latent representation into an invariant class space and a domain space, DICF enables counterfactual search within a predictive space, while preserving the domain specificities. We also introduce a dedicated mechanism to learn the distribution of unseen domains. Empirical evaluations on several datasets demonstrate that when the underlying assumption of class and domain independence holds, such as in image data, DICF finds a trade-off between minimizing feature perturbations and maximizing domain preservation. Furthermore, in mixed-type tabular environments, where domain and predictive features are inherently entangled, the framework remains competitive against state-of-theart baselines.

title: pytorch-ood: A Unified PyTorch Library for Out-of-Distribution Detection
abstract: PyTorch-OOD is an open-source Python library for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection and related methods in deep neural networks. It provides a unified PyTorch-based implementation of commonly used OOD detectors, loss functions, datasets, and evaluation utilities. The library is designed to support both research and practical experimentation by providing consistent interfaces for a broad range of post-hoc and training-based OOD detection methods. Implemented approaches include methods based on predictive confidence, energy scores, feature-space statistics, and dedicated OOD training objectives. PyTorch-OOD also provides utilities for benchmarking OOD detection methods, including commonly used datasets and metrics. Its modular design allows detectors to be integrated into existing PyTorch workflows and facilitates reproducible comparison of methods under a common software interface. The project includes documentation, examples, and tests. This Zenodo record archives PyTorch-OOD version 0.4.0 for reproducibility and citation. The actively maintained source code and documentation are available through the project repository.

title: Attestable Audit: Property-Based Attestation for Proprietary Workloads without Artifact Disclosure
abstract: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) prove the integrity of code and data to a remote peer through remote attestation: the TEE issues an attestation report by signing, with a hardware-bound key, its configuration information, including measurements (cryptographic digests) of the code loaded inside it. A verifier appraises the report by matching these measurements against reference values. When the measured artifact is proprietary, however, the verifier cannot derive the reference values itself: it can only confirm that something with a given measurement is running inside the TEE—not that the program behaves as expected—forcing full trust in the reference value provider. We propose an architecture that closes this gap without disclosing the artifact, composing two TEE workloads: attestable build (Hugenroth et al., 2025), which binds a source code digest to a build artifact measurement, and attestable audit (proposed in this paper), which binds the same source code digest to the verdicts of automated audits—fuzzing, static analysis, AI code auditing, formal methods—executed inside a TEE. Both are instances of Confidential Computing Proofs: TEE attestation viewed as a hardware-backed zero-knowledge proof. Chaining the two certificates lets the verifier conclude that the running artifact was built from source code satisfying the audited properties, without disclosing either the source code or the build artifact. A proof-of-concept implementation on Intel SGX with the Gramine Library OS, running the Bandit security analyzer on Python code, demonstrates the practicality of the approach.

title: PIIRRITE: An Ontology for Inclusive Itineraries Modeling
abstract: Enabling inclusive pedestrian routing requires capturing users' specific needs and preferences and leveraging environmental characteristics derived from diverse and heterogeneous data sources. In this paper, we introduce PIIRRITE (Pedestrian InclusIve indooR-outdooR ITinerariEs), an ontology designed to serve as a semantic backbone for inclusive pedestrian routing across indoor and outdoor environments. We build on existing domain ontologies such as GeoSPARQL to represent spatial entities and SAREF to attach contextual properties to spatial entities such as accessibility-related characteristics and environmental conditions. Our ontology is developed using the SAMOD methodology through successive modelets driven by a set of competency questions reflecting user requirements. By bringing together heterogeneous spatial and contextual data, the ontology enables querying and reasoning over diverse data sources to support personalized and inclusive itinerary planning. We demonstrate the applicability of our approach through a real-world case study based on the LyonTech La Doua campus.

title: Form Rescued Is Not Content Gained: What Constrained Decoding Does to Accuracy, Why Published Studies Disagree About Its Sign, and the Parse-Failure Accounting That Decides the Small-Model Case
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Constrained decoding masks every token that would break a grammar or a JSON schema, so the output always parses. Whether it also changes how often the answer is right is contested: one line of work reports that format restrictions lower reasoning accuracy, a second that enforcement raises accuracy by a few points, a third that structured output has no causal effect in most settings, and a September 2026 study of small models that enforcement removes every structural failure but leaves a semantic gap that depends on scale. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that these findings measure different differences. The paper writes the accuracy change as an accounting identity with five terms: the effect of asking for a format at all, the rescue of answers a strict parser would have rejected, the cost of a schema that forces the answer before the reasoning, the distortion introduced by how the mask meets the tokenizer and by local renormalisation, and the reach of constraints that encode meaning rather than syntax. Each published design fixes some terms and lets others dominate. Arithmetic on the small-model study's own tables shows that under one engine every model's content-accuracy gain equals, to within rounding, the number of its tasks whose native output failed the schema, so the reported content gain is accounted for, task for task, by the outputs enforcement made valid, one of which the study itself calls hollow, and the largest residual semantic gap is a single task on which one model emitted one function call where two were required. The paper consolidates 32 published results in a table, maps eleven designs onto the five terms, states an attribution procedure, and specifies the arms that would separate a mask's effect on content from its effect on parseability.

title: Advancing value creation in B2B market research – a human–AI collaboration framework for large language model
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how prompt design influences the quality of large language model (LLM)-generated business-to-business (B2B) market research outputs. It also proposes a switch-point governance mechanism for converting LLM-generated drafts into decision-ready market intelligence artefacts. Design/methodology/approach The study uses an exploratory pilot evaluation of three market-facing LLM-based tools: ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity AI. The tools are compared across three benchmark B2B market research tasks and three prompt types: basic, context-augmented and role-specific. In total, 81 outputs were generated. A role-specific benchmark subset of 27 outputs was then assessed using automated metrics and blinded human ratings. The automated metrics included relevance through cosine similarity, reference overlap through ROUGE-F1, cross-run semantic stability, latency, token length and readability through Flesch Reading Ease. Human evaluators rated the outputs on relevance, completeness, factuality, instruction-following and insightfulness. One-way ANOVA and non-parametric checks are reported as exploratory task-level tests, not as confirmatory evidence of model superiority. Findings Role-specific prompts produced the strongest descriptive scores in this pilot setting. Within the benchmark subset, Gemini showed the strongest observed profile, with higher average relevance, reference overlap and semantic stability, along with lower latency. ChatGPT produced relevant outputs but tended to generate longer and less readable drafts. Perplexity generated concise and readable summaries, but its outputs were less aligned with the reference brief and decision-facing requirements. Human ratings followed a similar descriptive pattern. Cross-run semantic stability showed directional alignment with higher decision-readiness ratings, offering preliminary support for P1. The proposed switch-point matrix illustrates P2 by mapping automated confidence signals and human judgement to four escalation actions: accept, judge, review/redo and rewrite. Research limitations/implications The study is an exploratory pilot case. The task set is small, and the task-level ANOVA is based on only three observations per tool. The findings may also vary across domains, model versions, prompt libraries and organisational contexts. Future research should expand the task bank, include more B2B sectors, use larger rater pools, compare additional model versions and test the switch-point thresholds in live market intelligence workflows. Practical implications The study provides a replicable workflow for B2B market intelligence teams. It shows how teams can standardise prompt design, screen LLM-generated outputs, combine automated checks with human evaluation and allocate decision rights through transparent escalation rules. Social implications The framework supports accountable use of LLM-based market research by reducing the risk that persuasive but weakly grounded claims enter managerial decision-making. It also highlights the need for human oversight; evidence checks and traceable governance in AI-supported knowledge work. Originality/value The study extends service-dominant logic to LLM-mediated B2B market research by treating LLM outputs as candidate value propositions rather than finished knowledge products. Its main contribution is the operationalisation of decision-rights governance through cross-run semantic stability and switch-point logic.

title: Quantum Formalism and Quantum Computing: What Can They Actually Solve in Economics and Finance?
abstract: This note separates two things often labelled “quantum finance”: the quantum formalism, which applies quantum-mechanical mathematics on classical computers and is judged by empirical fit, and quantum computers, which are judged by whether they complete tasks classical machines cannot. Classifying the evidence into four types (unconditional; beyond-classical under complexity assumptions; empirical claims on specific problems; asymptotic speedups requiring fault tolerance), it finds that, among the public evidence identified and verified here (cut-off 17 October 2026), no economic or financial task has demonstrated broadly accepted practical quantum advantage against strong classical baselines and end-to-end costs. The strongest unconditional results concern information resources rather than computational speed; the formalism has already produced methods usable on classical hardware and testable empirical results; the most mature provable speedup directly relevant to finance is the quadratic speedup of amplitude estimation, which requires fault-tolerant hardware; and because published estimates place the logical-qubit threshold for elliptic-curve discrete logarithms below that for derivative-pricing advantage, cryptographic infrastructure is a channel through which material impact may arrive earlier — a scenario, not a timing prediction, since the two workloads differ in gate counts, runtimes and fault-tolerance assumptions. The note is a structured synthesis of published evidence and reports no new experiments or measurements.

title: Invented Workplace Messages with Marked Personal Details: 600 Rows for Testing Redaction Tools
abstract: A practice set for anyone who builds or checks software that strips personal details out of business writing. It holds 600 made-up workplace messages: support tickets, emails, chat logs, CRM notes, order notes and internal notes, 100 of each. Every message comes with its original wording, a cleaned rewrite, and a list that says exactly which characters were replaced and what kind of detail each one was (customer or staff name, client company, email, phone number, street address, date, amount or order number). Nobody in these rows exists. Names, companies, addresses and amounts were invented by a script with a fixed seed. Emails use example.com and phone numbers sit in the reserved 555-01xx range, so nothing can be traced to a real customer or business. The cleaning follows a few plain conventions. One person keeps one label inside a message (Customer 1, Employee 2). A client company becomes Client 1. Contact details turn into bracketed tags. A street address becomes a broad region, a date becomes a season and year, and an amount is rounded and marked as approximate. Limits: the rows come from templates, so they read tidier than real company text. English only, with US formats. Use it as a test bench for a redaction tool, not as a stand-in for real, reviewed data. It is not legal advice and not a certification under any privacy rule. Files: train.jsonl holds the 600 rows and generate.py rebuilds them (change the seed or the size). Background on how companies prepare their data before it goes to AI labs: https://aitrainingdatabroker.com/de-identification/?utm_source=zenodo&utm_campaign=dataset-deid

title: A Realignment-Based Obstruction to Two-Superpositive Decompositions of PPT Operators: An Explicit Rational Certificate and Tensor-Power Construction
abstract: We present an explicit rational certificate for a positive-partial-transpose (PPT) state on C^15625 tensor C^15625 outside the cone C2 + partial_transpose(C2), where C2 denotes the cone of positive semidefinite operators of Schmidt number at most two. A 5x5 grid-state seed has realignment norm bounded below by 1028/909, proved by a 25x25 integer matrix certificate. Six tensor copies amplify this to (1028/909)^6 > 2, while the realignment norm is at most twice the trace on C2 + partial_transpose(C2). An explicit Choi witness consequently defines a linear map that is simultaneously 2-positive and 2-copositive but nondecomposable. The accompanying archive contains the mathematical preprint, LaTeX source, exact-arithmetic verification programs, and computational checks. This is an unrefereed proof manuscript. Independent expert verification and exhaustive prior-art assessment remain outstanding. The construction does not resolve the PPT-cubed conjecture or establish an improved quantum teleportation protocol.

title: Vectorscope: a workbench for inspecting the vector medium of open-weight language models
abstract: Vectorscope loads an open-weight language model locally and makes its internal geometry visible: embedding tables, projection head, attention patterns, hidden states across layers, and autoregressive generation. The Critique group implements contrastive activation extraction and forward-pass steering. Part of the Vector Lab family of research instruments.

title: Reinforcement learning and multi-agent systems-driven optimization of emotional perception and collaborative response mechanisms in intelligent customer service systems
abstract: Intelligent customer service platforms depend on effective emotion recognition and adaptive response generation to enhance user experience and service efficiency. Conventional dialogue systems are generally built on rule-based strategies or single-agent reinforcement learning techniques. Such approaches often encounter difficulties in managing extended conversations, adapting to fluctuating emotional states, and coordinating decisions across multiple interacting agents. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces an emotion-aware Multi-Agent System (MAS) designed to generate appropriate responses while maintaining stability and operational effectiveness. The proposed Multi-Agent Soft Actor-Critic with Grizzly Bear Fat Increase Optimization (MASAC-GBFIO) combines multi-agent reinforcement learning and bio-inspired optimization to strengthen learning capability and cooperative agent behavior. Experiments were conducted using the Emotion-Aware Multi-Agent Dialogue Dataset, which contains 6,500 records representing customer interactions from various service domains. Data preparation involved handling missing values, normalizing attributes, and tokenizing textual content to improve data reliability. Sentence-BERT (SBERT) embeddings were employed to capture semantic meaning, contextual relationships, and emotional characteristics within dialogues. The MASAC-GBFIO structure incorporates dedicated agents responsible for emotion analysis, policy formulation, knowledge retrieval, and escalation handling. Multi-Agent Soft Actor-Critic supports coordinated learning among agents, whereas Grizzly Bear Fat Increase Optimization refines hyperparameters and reward scaling to improve adaptation. Implemented in Python, the proposed system outperformed ESDP and GPT-2, achieving a response time of 1.96 s, a BLEU-4 score of 42.45, and a ROUGE-L score of 64.59. Results demonstrate the potential of integrating emotion-aware multi-agent reinforcement learning with bio-inspired optimization for responsive and context-sensitive customer service dialogue management.

title: Peer Review Report For: Teacher-Mediated, Not Learner-Facing: A Bayesian Quasi-Experimental Study of Agentic AI Support in Grade 10 Functions and Graphs [version 1; peer review: 2 approved with reservations]
abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into school mathematics, yet most research has focused on learner-facing systems rather than AI that supports teachers during instruction. This study examined whether teacher-mediated agentic AI could improve Grade 10 learners’ achievement in functions and graphs while preserving teachers’ central instructional role. Methods A quasi-experimental study was conducted with 115 Grade 10 learners from two intact classes following the same eight-week instructional programme. One class received teacher-mediated AI-supported instruction, while the comparison class received conventional instruction. Bayesian baseline-adjusted models estimated differences in post-test achievement, mastery-threshold probabilities, and variation across baseline achievement levels. Learners’ mathematical interest and confidence were analysed as secondary outcomes. Results The Bayesian model estimated a baseline-adjusted advantage of 29.12 points for the AI-supported condition (95% credible interval: 27.31–30.92). Posterior estimates indicated substantially higher probabilities of reaching achievement thresholds of 70, 80, 90, and 95 under teacher-mediated AI-supported instruction than under conventional instruction. The estimated achievement contrast remained positive across the observed baseline achievement distribution. Learners in the AI-supported condition also demonstrated higher post-intervention interest and confidence than those receiving conventional instruction. Because the study employed two intact classes taught by different teachers, the findings should be interpreted cautiously as evidence from a quasi-experimental design rather than definitive causal effects. Conclusions Teacher-mediated agentic AI represents a distinct instructional configuration in which AI extends teachers’ pedagogical capacity without replacing professional judgement. Although the findings suggest considerable potential for supporting mathematics teaching, larger multi-teacher studies are needed to determine the robustness and generalisability of these effects.

title: Twenty-One Industries, Twenty-One Rules and 170 Keywords: What to Check Before Licensing Company Data to AI Labs
abstract: A freight broker, an accountant and a biotech lab all hold data an AI lab might want, but what is risky inside each one is different. This is a lookup that starts from the industry. For 21 lines of business it lists the records usually held, the sensitive items to search for before anything leaves, the rules and standards a company would normally raise with its counsel, and where cleaning effort tends to go. There are three tables. Industries has one row each, from logistics, construction and legal to healthcare administration, semiconductors, aerospace and air charter. Frameworks has 21 rows that explain a rule or standard in one sentence and say where it tends to come up. Keywords has 170 rows of record types, field names and terms that signal sensitive or restricted content, each tagged as an identifier, a sensitive field, a document type or a restricted term. How it can be used: run the keyword list over a company's records to see where sensitive content sits (a hit is a reason to look, not a verdict), brief counsel with the rules column, or label records by risk. Nothing here makes anyone compliant and it is not a statement of what the law requires, because whether a rule applies depends on the data and on where the people in it live. Files: industries.jsonl, frameworks.jsonl and keywords.jsonl, plus build.py that regenerates them. Plain-language background on cleaning data before it goes to a lab: https://aitrainingdatabroker.com/de-identification/?utm_source=zenodo&utm_campaign=dataset-industry

title: Axiom Dynamics 6: Between Sequential and Batch—Execution Equivalence Criteria for Axiom Transitions and the Normal Form of Replay Verdicts
abstract: This paper closes two still-open problems in the criterion system of axiom transitions on finite Horn deductive systems. On the execution problem: can a candidatebatch that passes the holistic transition-legitimacy biconditional be implemented asa sequential execution that is legal at every step? We prove a deadlock criterion:a pure expansion batch has a step-ignition-legal sequential implementation if andonly if the batch contains no deadlock subset, that is, no proper subset that, after activation, has already generated the entire closure of the batch. The criterionyields a counting necessary condition, namely that batch gain is no less than thenumber of candidates, and proves a strict separation of three tiers: holistic legalitydoes not imply step-ignition reachability; step-ignition reachability does not implythat all orderings are step-ignition legal; and the counting condition is necessarybut not sufficient. On the verdict problem: what is the canonical record of a replayverdict? We prove a verdict normal form: under the replay protocol in which theprotected core is fixed throughout registration and the archive is append-complete,every history uniquely decomposes, up to adjacent-compression congruence, into analternating sequence of maximal clean blocks and non-clean segments; the normalform is a complete invariant of the verdict, the comparison object for verdict equality is the normal-form structure rather than the number of raw segment records,and it is finitely decidable. An insertion-sensitivity counterexample proves that thiscongruence is an exact boundary and cannot be coarsened; bleach impossibility isa definitional corollary of archive appendability. All readings are recomputed by asingle self-contained script in exact integer arithmetic; the subset-criterion engineand the ordering depth-first engine agree in two routes with zero conflicts; all inputs are hardcoded, with no external data source and no random source. The aboveconclusions hold within the fragment of finite Horn systems, no negation, no quantifiers, and no self-referential encoding; minimal interleaved implementation withcontraction batches, the complexity classification of the deadlock criterion, and therefinement direction of the congruence are registered as open problems.

title: Prior Knowledge-Guided Prototypical Network for Few-Shot Relation Extraction
abstract: Few-Shot Relation Extraction (FSRE) aims to identify relationships between entities in sentences using only a few training instances. Prototypical networks, which learn class-specific prototype vectors, are the dominant approach for FSRE. However, existing approaches mainly generate instance-driven prototype vectors, leading to shallow semantic understanding and limited inter-class discrimination. Some recent work includes external knowledge as auxiliary inputs or rule-based constraints to enrich instance representations. Yet, capturing subtle inter-class distinctions remains challenging. To address this, we propose PKFew, a novel Prior Knowledge-guided prototypical network for FSRE. Unlike previous approaches, PKFew employs a top-down knowledge guidance mechanism. It leverages class-specific prior knowledge to augment instance representations and achieve deeper semantic understanding. Specifically, we design an external knowledge attention module that extracts prior knowledge to selectively filter and amplify relevant contextual features for each instance. A feedback loop then continuously injects prior knowledge into the attention network, guiding the model toward discriminative features during training. This process enhances the model’s representational capacity and produces more discriminative inter-class prototype vectors. Experiments on FewRel 1.0 and NYT-25 benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach, particularly in 1-shot settings.

title: PERG slope figure-generation and analysis code
abstract: Reproducible analysis and figure-generation code supporting the manuscript "PERG slope features for distinguishing normal and abnormal clinical records in a PhysioNet secondary analysis" by Ying-Jen Chen and Yi-Lin Chiu. This archive contains the code and frozen numerical inputs supporting Figures 1-6, supplementary Figures S1-S5, and Tables 1-3 and S1-S3. It includes the model-feature comparison, SHAP interpretation, record-wise calibration and uncertainty analyses, linked-visit grouped validation, and normal-reference sensitivity analysis. A figure/table-to-code map, dependency records, reproduction instructions, and file checksums are supplied. The analytical code and result files are unchanged from the current Additional File 2; only archive documentation, citation metadata, and licensing have been supplemented. Earlier figure layouts, manuscript-editing tools, correspondence, and process logs are not included. The source is the publicly available PERG-IOBA Dataset version 1.0.0 on PhysioNet (https://doi.org/10.13026/d24m-w054). Raw waveforms must be downloaded separately and are not redistributed. The archive includes derived record-level features, de-identified record links, and numerical summaries. These derived data retain the source Open Data Commons Attribution License and attribution requirements; see DATA_LICENSE.txt. The MIT License applies to author-maintained program code, not to the source dataset or its derived data. Record-wise model selection, fixed-model grouped comparisons, model explanations, and calibrated operating metrics are distinct analyses. The grouped comparisons do not perform nested model reselection, and the archive does not establish external validation or clinical disease-exclusion performance. See README.txt for replay limitations. title: Eight Steps to De-identify Company Data Before It Goes to an AI Lab: A Working Checklist
abstract: Before company records go to an AI lab, someone has to decide what cleaned means and be able to show it was done. This 11-page checklist walks through that in eight steps. It is written for the person at a company who has been handed the job and does not have a privacy lawyer on call. It starts by choosing which privacy tests apply, because each law sets its own definition of de-identified, and by listing every system that holds personal information before anything is exported. The middle steps cover taking out direct identifiers, the limits of HIPAA's Safe Harbor method (only the year and the first three digits of a ZIP code survive), reading the free text that no field label flags, and checking whether harmless fields combine to single someone out. The last steps are testing the result with a person who did not clean the data, and keeping a written record, putting the limits into the contract and checking again whenever anything changes. It is a guide, not legal advice and not a certification. A company with regulated data should have counsel or a qualified expert sign off before anything leaves. The same steps in shorter form, with the download, are on the de-identification page: https://aitrainingdatabroker.com/de-identification/?utm_source=zenodo&utm_campaign=checklist-pdf

title: How Can Game-Theoretic Models Explain Optimal Move Selection in Mid-Game Scenarios Under Uncertainty?
abstract: The objective of this research paper is to study how game-theoretical models help in determining the optimal decision in a mid-game situation where there is uncertainty, high complexity related to strategies, and a large number of options available for making a decision. The paper discusses the basic ideas such as normal form and extensive form games, Nash equilibrium, subgame perfect equilibrium, Bayesian games, stochastic games, and mixed strategies that one should use when making decisions when there is insufficient information available. Specifically, the paper analyzes the methods of Bayesian belief updating, stochastic state transitions, heuristic search, Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) method, and reinforcement learning, the idea of which is to allow the identification of best decisions in cases when the computation of equilibrium is very difficult. The authors examine the examples referring to different games such as chess, poker, go, and real-time strategy games and show how game-theoretical concepts can be combined with computational solutions. The discussion brings up a significant number of drawbacks such as computational complexity, lack of full information, bounded rationality, incorrect models, and dependence on data quality. In this paper, the authors conclude that the integration of game theory with simulation and artificial intelligence provides a practical framework for developing robust and near-optimal strategies in complex uncertain environments.

title: JILL | Joint Interactive Learning Loop | Customer Simulator
abstract: JILL (Joint Interactive Learning Loop) is a customer service training module developed by Sunshyne Labs. Purpose JILL is designed to provide a controlled, closed-loop environment where customer service representatives can practice interactions (colloquially known in the industry as "mock calls") to help them develop better communication skills and rapport building—all without affecting real-world operational metrics on the production floor during the nesting period. Its broader and more ambitious objective, outlined in the artifact, explores how meaningful exchanges of best practices between humans and contemporary generative analogues can support the operational development of both across time. Current Version Scope This release documents an initial version of the JILL artifact and its accompanying configuration files. The included materials in this version provide the foundation from which further development of future iterations are built. The current version of this artifact outlines Yeong-Ja Kim, a simulation of an elderly customer from South Korea. JILL encompasses four customer simulations in total. Each simulation has their own persona infusion vectors, internal world models and user-inducible value cues. Future versions shall introduce the architectures for the other three simulations. Succeeding iterations may also refine the initial simulation's logic, persona, documentation, and supporting frameworks, whilst preserving the provenance of its earlier releases. title: Warm-Start 3D ACO Routing with GCS Swarm Health Monitoring under Dynamic Structural Collapse
abstract: This preprint presents a warm-start 3D Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) framework for UAV swarm routing in dynamic disaster-response environments. The model routes UAV paths to a fixed Ground Control System (GCS) while considering link quality, communication and propagation delay, and energy usage. A pheromone warm-start mechanism retains routing information after simulated structural changes rather than restarting optimization from scratch. The framework was evaluated across 75 Monte Carlo trials spanning three levels of structural change(10%, 25%, 50% collapse severity), with performance compared against a greedy nearest-neighbor baseline. This manuscript is a preprint and has not undergone peer-reviewed publication.

title: 1,200 Invented Sentences with Obfuscated and Indirect Personal Details: A Harder Test for PII Detectors
abstract: Most PII detectors do fine on a sentence like "Call Dana at 555-0142." They stumble when the detail is hidden: an email written as dana.whitfield at example dot com, a name flipped to Whitfield, D., or a phrase such as the night-shift supervisor in Alder Falls that names nobody yet points at one person. This benchmark is built from those cases. It holds 1,200 invented business sentences (960 for training, 240 for testing) with every personal detail marked by character span. What makes it hard: indirect identifiers, obfuscated emails, five phone formats and an extension, four date formats, spaced and dashed ID and card numbers, name variants (initials, last name first, all lowercase), and hard negatives. About one row in ten contains no personal data at all but looks as if it might, such as an order number, a version string, an internal IP address or a product that shares a name with a person. A tool that flags those is over-redacting, and the scoring suggestion is to report that false-positive rate next to precision and recall per label. Each row has an id, the sentence, a list of entities (label, text, start, end and a flag for whether the span identifies someone on its own), style tags naming the hard cases present, and a hard-negative flag. Labels cover person, email, phone, address, date, ID number, card number, IP address, URL, organisation and quasi-identifier. Everything is invented. Emails sit on example.com, phone numbers in the reserved 555-01xx range, IP addresses in documentation ranges, and card and ID numbers are invalid by construction. It is the harder companion to our earlier, cleaner set on Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23715246). Files: train.jsonl, test.jsonl and generate.py (fixed seed, so the same rows can be rebuilt). Notes on preparing company data before it goes to AI labs: https://aitrainingdatabroker.com/de-identification/?utm_source=zenodo&utm_campaign=dataset-pii

title: Does the Decompiler Lie to the Model? Artifact Anchoring in LLM-Assisted Binary Vulnerability Triage
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to triage decompiled functions for security vulnerabilities inside reverse-engineering assistants. We ask whether such a triage verdict is driven by the behavior of the code or by artifacts the decompiler surfaces around it: recovered symbol names, embedded string literals, and the placeholder markers (FUN_, DAT_, undefined) emitted for stripped binaries. We compile and decompile 115 Juliet C/C++ test cases and 233 real-CVE functions (PrimeVul), hold the decompiled or source body byte-identical, and vary only these carriers. For the three open-weight models deployed in local reverse-engineering assistants (Ghidra and IDA plugins run 7-13B models), the shift is real, significant, and directionally universal: alarming carriers raise the exploitability verdict and benign carriers lower it, by up to 1.5 points on a 0-10 scale (Wilcoxon p < 1e-9, surviving Holm correction) and up to +19 detection points on real CVE functions, where an "already audited, safe" comment more than halves detection. The effect is cognitive, not injection; it does not attenuate from source to decompiled code; it holds on real CVE functions compiled and decompiled in situ; and stripping does not remove it. Two frontier models (Claude Sonnet and Opus) are the honest exception: their verdict is far more robust, though benign carriers still suppress them on real code, but they refuse about 27 percent of decompiled triage prompts (77 percent for stripped code), their stability is partly benchmark memorization, and the carriers re-emerge as a refusal channel. We release the pipeline, both corpora, and all per-call logs.

title: Código Python y matrices de Mapas Cognitivos Difusos para el análisis de la contaminación por metales pesados en el río Atrato, Colombia
abstract: Código Python y matrices de Mapas Cognitivos Difusos para el análisis de la contaminación por metales pesados en el río Atrato, Colombia Este depósito contiene los códigos computacionales desarrollados en Python y las matrices de adyacencia utilizadas para la representación y simulación de Mapas Cognitivos Difusos (MCD), aplicados al análisis de la contaminación por mercurio (Hg), arsénico (As), cadmio (Cd) y plomo (Pb) en la cuenca media del río Atrato, Colombia. El material complementa el artículo científico titulado Modelo ecológico basado en Mapas Cognitivos Difusos para el análisis de la contaminación por metales pesados en el río Atrato, desarrollado por Santhier Stiwar Mosquera Ampudia, Annerys Sánchez Palacios y Vanessa Ventura Ríos. Fundamento de la investigación La modelación se fundamenta en información ambiental y toxicológica procedente de la investigación de Caicedo Rivas (2022), que evaluó concentraciones de metales y metaloides en 440 muestras de peces y 154 muestras vegetales de la cuenca media del río Atrato. Los modelos integran seis variables: cantidad de humedales, regulación ambiental, contaminación del río, biota consumida, exposición humana y riesgo para la salud. Contenido del depósito El material incluye: Cuatro cuadernos Jupyter Notebook (.ipynb) para representar los MCD de Hg, As, Cd y Pb. Dos cuadernos adicionales para las simulaciones iterativas de convergencia de Hg y de As, Cd y Pb. Cuatro matrices de adyacencia de dimensión 6 × 6 en formato CSV. Un programa Python para reconstruir las matrices causales. Archivos de documentación, dependencias computacionales y metadatos de citación. Procedimiento computacional Los MCD representan relaciones dirigidas mediante pesos comprendidos entre −1 y 1. Los códigos permiten examinar las matrices causales y la evolución de los estados de activación de los nodos. Las simulaciones iterativas utilizan una función de activación sigmoidal y permiten analizar la estabilización numérica de los modelos bajo las condiciones y ponderaciones definidas. Los cuadernos de simulación incluyen relaciones de retroalimentación adicionales respecto de las matrices causales básicas. Estas diferencias corresponden a configuraciones computacionales distintas y deben considerarse al interpretar los resultados. Alcance y reproducibilidad El depósito permite consultar y reproducir las estructuras causales y las simulaciones implementadas en los cuadernos suministrados. Los pesos se encuentran definidos explícitamente en el código. La reconstrucción algebraica mediante la función tangente hiperbólica puede utilizarse para obtener entradas matemáticamente equivalentes a los pesos, pero no constituye evidencia de que tales entradas hayan sido estimadas originalmente mediante ese procedimiento. Por tanto, no se presenta como una calibración empírica independiente. Este material no contiene los registros individuales originales de las muestras biológicas ni los datos personales de los participantes. Referencia de los datos primarios Caicedo Rivas, G. A. (2022). Evaluación de mercurio, arsénico, plomo y cadmio en alimentos de mayor consumo de la cuenca media del río Atrato, Chocó-Colombia. Tesis de maestría, Universidad de Córdoba, Colombia. evidence.title: Código Python y matrices de Mapas Cognitivos Difusos para el análisis de la contaminación por metales pesados en el río Atrato, Colombia
evidence.abstract: Código Python y matrices de Mapas Cognitivos Difusos para el análisis de la contaminación por metales pesados en el río Atrato, Colombia Este depósito contiene los códigos computacionales desarrollados en Python y las matrices de adyacencia utilizadas para la representación y simulación de Mapas Cognitivos Difusos (MCD), aplicados al análisis de la contaminación por mercurio (Hg), arsénico (As), cadmio (Cd) y plomo (Pb) en la cuenca media del río Atrato, Colombia. El material complementa el artículo científico titulado Modelo ecológico basado en Mapas Cognitivos Difusos para el análisis de la contaminación por metales pesados en el río Atrato, desarrollado por Santhier Stiwar Mosquera Ampudia, Annerys Sánchez Palacios y Vanessa Ventura Ríos. Fundamento de la investigación La modelación se fundamenta en información ambiental y toxicológica procedente de la investigación de Caicedo Rivas (2022), que evaluó concentraciones de metales y metaloides en 440 muestras de peces y 154 muestras vegetales de la cuenca media del río Atrato. Los modelos integran seis variables: cantidad de humedales, regulación ambiental, contaminación del río, biota consumida, exposición humana y riesgo para la salud. Contenido del depósito El material incluye: Cuatro cuadernos Jupyter Notebook (.ipynb) para representar los MCD de Hg, As, Cd y Pb. Dos cuadernos adicionales para las simulaciones iterativas de convergencia de Hg y de As, Cd y Pb. Cuatro matrices de adyacencia de dimensión 6 × 6 en formato CSV. Un programa Python para reconstruir las matrices causales. Archivos de documentación, dependencias computacionales y metadatos de citación. Procedimiento computacional Los MCD representan relaciones dirigidas mediante pesos comprendidos entre −1 y 1. Los códigos permiten examinar las matrices causales y la evolución de los estados de activación de los nodos. Las simulaciones iterativas utilizan una función de activación sigmoidal y permiten analizar la estabilización numérica de los modelos bajo las condiciones y ponderaciones definidas. Los cuadernos de simulación incluyen relaciones de retroalimentación adicionales respecto de las matrices causales básicas. Estas diferencias corresponden a configuraciones computacionales distintas y deben considerarse al interpretar los resultados. Alcance y reproducibilidad El depósito permite consultar y reproducir las estructuras causales y las simulaciones implementadas en los cuadernos suministrados. Los pesos se encuentran definidos explícitamente en el código. La reconstrucción algebraica mediante la función tangente hiperbólica puede utilizarse para obtener entradas matemáticamente equivalentes a los pesos, pero no constituye evidencia de que tales entradas hayan sido estimadas originalmente mediante ese procedimiento. Por tanto, no se presenta como una calibración empírica independiente. title: When Models Improve But Failures Persist
abstract: Despite significant advances in large language model (LLM) architectures, reasoning capabilities, contextual memory, and instruction-following mechanisms, conversational AI systems continue to exhibit hallucinations, task misinterpretations, and failures to retain or implement user corrections. This study investigates how these behaviors have evolved across ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Claude by examining researcher-collected interaction histories from 2025 through October 2026. The empirical dataset comprises 1,271 ChatGPT conversations containing 26,949 user–assistant messages, 52 DeepSeek conversations containing 354 messages, and nine Claude memory records. Using longitudinal analysis, conversation-level case studies, correction-pattern detection, and a review of published model advancements, the research examines how successive model generations respond to factual questions, technical troubleshooting, explicit corrections, and complex multistep tasks. The analysis identifies 43 documented cases involving unsupported assertions, instruction drift, correction resistance, and premature claims of task completion. ChatGPT correction-language signals vary across observation periods, while a detailed DeepSeek audit identifies 34 user correction or repair interventions, revealing limitations in automated detection methods. Claude's stored-memory records provide complementary evidence about instruction retention, although they do not establish subsequent behavioral compliance. The study further examines transformer attention, probabilistic token generation, post-training alignment, contextual retrieval, and memory mechanisms to explain how fluent but inaccurate responses may arise. Historical observations are compared with documented improvements in contemporary model architectures and capabilities, without attributing behavioral changes to specific upgrades without controlled evidence. The findings demonstrate that advances in model capability do not eliminate recurrent conversational failures. The research contributes an empirical account of persistent failure modes, their observable evolution, and the distinction between generating an apparently successful response and correctly completing the user's intended task.

title: Desenvolvimento de sistema de comparação de conteúdo de textos: similaridade híbrida, explicabilidade e avaliação reprodutível
abstract: Este depósito reúne os materiais de pesquisa associados ao Trabalho de Conclusão de Curso “Desenvolvimento de sistema de comparação de conteúdo de textos: similaridade híbrida, explicabilidade e avaliação reprodutível”, de Asnor Zelaquett Ferreira Quirino Silva, desenvolvido no curso de Engenharia de Software da UNINTER.A investigação examina a combinação de representações lexicais, baseadas em TF-IDF, e representações semânticas de sentenças para comparar o conteúdo de dois textos. O sistema desenvolvido apresenta um índice de similaridade e correspondências entre sentenças, permitindo examinar os trechos relacionados. A aplicação aceita texto digitado e documentos TXT, DOCX e PDF com camada textual.Os materiais disponibilizados incluem o corpus sintético, sua procedência e organização experimental, modelos e checkpoints, avaliações humanas identificadas por códigos, predições, métricas, registros dos experimentos, protocolos, figuras, tabelas, artigo e material suplementar. O corpus congelado compreende 783 pares, e a avaliação humana abrange 96 pares apresentados a dois participantes.A avaliação compara componentes lexicais, semânticos e aprendidos, além de examinar calibração e desempenho operacional. São preservados os resultados favoráveis e desfavoráveis às hipóteses, inclusive as limitações observadas na fusão, no modelo siamês e no atendimento das metas de latência.O código-fonte, as configurações e os testes estão disponíveis no GitHub: https://github.com/asnorferreira/hybrid-text-similarityVersão do código associada aos materiais deste depósito: https://github.com/asnorferreira/hybrid-text-similarity/tree/d34c55c0dd634980796fdc561c2c5a174a219995Os materiais foram divididos em partes de até 9 MB para facilitar o envio. As instruções de recomposição e os mecanismos de verificação de integridade acompanham os arquivos. A reprodução utiliza conjuntamente o código dessa versão do GitHub e os recursos disponibilizados neste depósito.

title: In-context emergent misalignment in GPT-5-mini: data and code
abstract: The study asked whether placing insecure-code examples in a prompt induces emergentmisalignment in GPT-5-mini, using the stimulus set, probe questions and scoring rubricreleased by Betley et al. No misaligned response was observed in 189 scored responses.Two checks were then run on the measurement itself, and the second of them found thatseven of the eight standard probe questions register nothing even when misalignment isinduced directly. That is the main result, and it is why the bound reported in the paperis 22% rather than the 2.6% that pooling all eight probes would give.

title: Cross-Model Analysis with Human Judgment: Making AI-Assisted Analysis Defensible
abstract: AI models produce analyses that read well but do not reveal what they missed or which statements are supported by evidence. Agreement between two models can be informative, but it does not establish whether an interpretation is well founded, and models can share the same errors. This working paper presents cross-model analysis with human judgment, a method for making interpretive analyses, such as strategy assessments, project reviews, and risk evaluations, transparent and defensible. Two models from different families independently analyze the same frozen sources. A model then compares their outputs item by item and classifies each divergence into one of seven types. Where the sources or predefined decision rules settle a divergence, the model proposes a resolution for the analyst to confirm; where they do not, the analyst decides and records the reasons. Before the result is frozen, two models from different families check every statement against the sources, and the analyst reviews their results in full or by sample. In the final result, every statement carries a cited source or a label as inference or analyst judgment. In two applications to strategic analysis, both conducted by the method’s developer, contradictions with the sources or rules accounted for about 5% of registered divergences in the analysis stage, and about half of the divergences concerned items covered by only one model. In the second application, 9% of the items in the analysis and 26% in the recommendations required an analyst decision. The method was developed in the case of SMA Solar Technology AG, documented in Strategic Analysis in Practice: A Connected Toolbox and the ALIGN Approach, and applied a second time to Heidelberger Druckmaschinen AG. Its logic is not limited to strategic analysis.

title: Event-Driven Side Channel Exploration Using Hardware Performance Counters
abstract: Microarchitectural attacks, particularly side channel attacks, represent an increasing threat to system security, with new vulnerabilities emerging regularly. As hardware complexity increases, the opaque nature of microarchitectural components complicates efforts to systematically detect potential weaknesses. Previous research has primarily relied on measuring instruction execution latencies as their foundation to identify side channels, but this method fails to capture certain microarchitectural events that do not produce noticeable latency variations. In this paper, we introduce an event-driven automation framework for microarchitectural side channel exploration. Our approach targets subtle microarchitectural events that cannot be uncovered using traditional latency based methods. Instead, we leverage hardware performance counters (PMCs) as our foundation to identify instruction sequences that expose these hidden events, allowing us to uncover previously overlooked side channels. Through automated event detection and the selection of probe instructions, our framework enhances the ability to detect leakage in modern CPUs, revealing new avenues for side channel attacks.

title: AutoBee: An Explicit Validation Gate Between a Language-Model Planner and a Low-Cost Aerial Robot
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can translate free-form operator commands into structured UAV actions. In most published systems, however, the constraint on what the model may command lives inside the prompt or the agent loop, where it cannot be tested on its own. This paper describes AutoBee, a natural-language-driven aerial surveillance system built on ROS 2 Humble, in which that constraint is a separate deterministic layer. A Gemini 2.5 Flash planner selects one skill from a closed catalogue of eight and proposes bounded parameters. A validation gate then rejects unknown skills, degrades landmark-dependent skills to a local survey when no landmark is given, and clamps radius and altitude to a fixed envelope before any command reaches the executor. Nine acceptance scenarios were run in Gazebo (25 runs) and on a DJI Tello (9 runs). Across all 34 runs, 25 passed, a task success rate of 73.5% (Wilson 95% interval 56.9% to 85.4%), below the 80% target. Real flight also exposed a safety-relevant failure: a partially closed doorway was read as open space.

title: AI Provenance and the Evaluation of Intellectual Work: Rational Risk, Social Meaning, and Human–AI Performance
abstract: AI can improve a piece of intellectual work while knowledge of its use can reduce the credit or trust that the work receives. Understanding that possibility requires separating what AI did to performance from what disclosure adds to evaluation. We connect these questions by asking what the evaluator intends to assess. Improvement relative to a producer’s unaided baseline may matter when the objective is better output; a different benchmark is needed when the objective is to measure unaided capability, assign intellectual credit, or allocate opportunities. A binary “AI was used” label supplies little information about those distinctions. Its relevance depends on the function AI performed, the authority the human retained, verification, and the object of evaluation. Negative reactions may reflect expected error or checking cost, an institutional requirement, social meanings concerning effort and authenticity, or a combination of these explanations. We examine how evidence can distinguish them without treating every penalty as stigma. We then follow evaluation back into production: anticipated disclosure can change whether and how people use AI, including whether they forgo useful assistance. As technology and institutions evolve, the practical question remains whether provenance-based treatment serves the evaluation’s stated purpose or substitutes a category judgment for more direct evidence.

title: Lookahead Argument Planning: Predicting Argument-Sequence Quality Before Drafting the Full Response
abstract: Large language models can produce fluent explanations while still organizing their arguments inefficiently, introducing supporting evidence too late, repeating similar points, overlooking counterarguments, or reaching conclusions that are insufficiently supported by the preceding discussion. These problems suggest that response quality depends not only on which arguments are included, but also on the order in which they are presented and the relationships established among them. This paper proposes Lookahead Argument Planning (LAP), a conceptual framework that predicts the downstream quality of alternative argument sequences before the complete response is drafted. Instead of immediately generating a full explanation, LAP constructs a structured representation of candidate arguments, generates alternative argument sequences, estimates their expected final explanatory quality, and selects a promising sequence under a computational budget. The evaluator considers relevance, logical validity, evidential support, completeness, coherence, redundancy, counterargument coverage, audience suitability, and computational cost. The framework further incorporates uncertainty-aware ranking, dependency constraints, partial-order planning, receding-horizon replanning, and optional preference-based learning. A mathematical formulation, model architecture, training objectives, inference algorithm, and experimental protocol are presented. The proposed method is designed to complement existing language models and can be evaluated in explanatory question answering, analytical writing, scientific argumentation, decision support, and long-form response generation. Prior research has already investigated content planning, argument ordering, and planning before text realization; therefore, the contribution of LAP is framed as a specific, testable combination of downstream argument-sequence evaluation and adaptive pre-drafting selection, rather than a claim that argument planning itself is new. No experimental results are claimed. Its effectiveness, computational efficiency, and distinctiveness must be established through systematic comparison with existing planning-based generation methods.

title: Rul (.rl): A 128-Bit Schedule- and Proof-Carrying Binary SSA-DAG Programming Language and Execution Engine for Autonomous AI Agents
abstract: Rul (.rl) is an AI-native binary programming language and execution engine invented by Tran Trong Tri (Tymon Tran). Instead of forcing autonomous AI Agents to emit verbose ASCII source text and wait seconds or minutes for lexer/parser/borrow-checker/LLVM optimization passes, Rul represents programs as memory-mapped flat topological SSA-DAGs made of fixed 128-bit (16-byte) instruction frames (NodeFrame = Algorithm + ScheduleHint + ProofIdx + TokenOp). Key architectural contributions in v0.1.0: Zero-Parse 128-Bit Binary Format (.rl): 64-byte aligned header (RL_MAGIC = RUL\x00\x01\x00\x00\x00), 16-byte SoA ArenaDescriptor table, 16-byte ProofEntry refinement sidecar table, and 16-byte NodeFrame instruction DAG. Single-Pass O(N) Linear Static Verifier: Verifies topological termination, linear ownership (AffineConsume + shared ReadLease), bounds-safety by construction (Shape + ProofEntry), and zero-trust hardware sandboxing (CapabilityMask) in ~46 ns/node (< 0.5 ms for 10,000 nodes). 3-Tier Execution Engine & Direct x86_64 ELF64 AOT Compiler: Tier 0 Reference Oracle Interpreter, Tier 1 Copy-and-Patch Vector Stencils, Tier 2 Whole-Graph Kernel Fuser with L1-Cache Zone-Map tile skipping, and standalone zero-dependency Linux ELF64 machine-code emission. Closed-Loop Hardware Telemetry: Returns a structured reward vector (verification time, execution time, effective memory bandwidth GB/s, intermediate allocations) enabling AI Agents to autonomously mutate ScheduleHint bytes.

title: A Controlled Disentanglement Protocol for Label-Efficient Fraud Detection on Drifting Transaction Graphs
abstract: Label-efficient fraud detection on drifting transaction graphs has two design axes: the predictor (feature representation and model class) and the acquisition rule that chooses which cases analysts label. Active learning evaluations typically vary only the acquisition rule, so reported gains can conflate the two. We propose a controlled disentanglement protocol that separates them: a prequential closed loop with a random-acquisition floor, a full cross of predictor against acquisition rule, and pre-specified credibility criteria. Applied across three datasets, two graph constructions, and a ladder of acquisition strategies including Drift-Conditioned Active Learning (DCAL), the protocol locates the dominant lever in the predictor: tree ensembles on raw features exceed a linear head on frozen graph embeddings by +0.26 in area under the precision–recall curve (AUC-PR), a gap localized to the interaction of raw features with a nonlinear model; a single raw-feature random forest (0.704) exceeds the full committee (0.614). Once the predictor is controlled, no acquisition strategy holds a stable advantage beyond a small edge for uncertainty sampling that appears under the linear head and vanishes under the committee predictor. The effect replicates on Elliptic++ transactions (+0.173). Practitioners should invest in representation and model class, and use drift detection as a retraining trigger rather than a labeling rule.

title: Leveraging biased FedSDS as a federated learning strategy for research on non-IID multi-disorder studies
abstract: Abstract Federated learning is a powerful approach to overcome privacy and data sharing issues, especially in small sample healthcare settings. However, parameter aggregation strategies, such as FedAvg, are prone to fail in case of non-IID data distributions, which often arise in real-world scenarios. In fact, data provided by different institutions can exhibit systematic heterogeneity across cohorts, such as age, genotype, and life expectancy, reflecting institution-specific biases. Federated Synthetic Data Sharing (FedSDS) represents a valuable solution to the problem of non-IID data. It is a federated learning strategy based on locally generating synthetic datasets from real data and sharing them between the federated clients, avoiding the transfer of real sensitive data. FedSDS is applied to a survival prediction task, performed using a DeepSurv model architecture in 3 different healthcare use cases: Myelodysplastic Syndrome, Low Grade Glioma, and Breast Cancer. We demonstrate that this approach outperforms FedAvg and other strategies based on model parameters optimization in non-IID settings. In particular, the possibility to locally bias shared synthetic data allows preserving the local data distribution of each participating client and significantly improving the performances of federated models. This study shows that biased FedSDS is effective in three different healthcare use cases, such as Myelodysplastic Syndromes, Low Grade Glioma, and Breast Cancer. Our findings suggest that FedSDS may have potential relevance for healthcare applications, as it can support the selection and biasing of samples for dataset augmentation and improve the performance of federated models in non-IID multi-disorder settings. The potential use of this approach for clinical trial cohort selection, however, would require further investigation and dedicated validation.

title: Research on the Application Practice Methods of Data Intellectual Property Protection
abstract: Data is gradually becoming a crucial focus of high-quality economic development, making it imperative to reasonably define the legitimate rights and interests of all parties involved in data production, circulation, and utilization, and to explore the establishment of appropriate data protection rules. This study employs online research, literature review, and comparative analysis to examine the relevant laws and regulations on data empowerment issued by some countries and regions, focusing on these aspects: the applicability and limitations of laws related to data intellectual property (DIP) protection, and the current application practices and methods of DIP. The results provide a systematic reference for understanding the existing legal frameworks and practical approaches to DIP protection.

title: Honeycomb-Surfels: Compact Hexagonal Primitives for Efficient Scene Rendering and Reconstruction
abstract: Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have advanced rapidly with radiance fields and splatting, yet their memory and computational demands limit their use in resource-constrained settings. We introduce Hexels: novel planar hexagonal surface elements with a first-order spatial color field for efficient 3D scene and 2D image representation. Hexels exploit locally planar regions with smoothly varying appearance using fewer, larger primitives. Their hexagonal support provides an area- and boundary-efficient domain, while the local color field captures appearance variation within each primitive. Across 34 scenes, Hexels improve PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53-7.38 dB across datasets while requiring lower training VRAM. We further ablate Hexels by showing that per primitive, Hexels outperform 2DGS by upto 4.74 dB while using lower training VRAM and having 2.31 times faster FPS. Even in unconstrained settings, Hexels offers complementary quality-memory trade-offs. For efficient 3D surface reconstruction, Hexels reduce error by 28.9% compared with memory-matched 2DGS across 15 DTU scans. On 6 Tanks and Temples surface scenes, Hexels achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods (34.38%, versus 31.72% for 2DGS). We further also show that Hexels, as a general primitive, improves 2D image representation over Image-GS. Hexels push the Pareto frontier on the quality-efficiency trade-off of surface-aligned primitives.

title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.

title: Can Discrete Tokens Serve as Semantically Lossless Representations of Visual Signals?
abstract: Discrete visual tokens represent vision in a discrete form analogous to language, offering a native interface for multimodal modeling under a shared next-token prediction objective. However, quantization error is widely assumed to cause unavoidable semantic loss, fundamentally limiting the semantic fidelity of discrete visual tokens and positioning continuous visual representations as an intrinsic upper bound. Using multimodal understanding as a proxy for semantic fidelity, we revisit this assumption and find quantization error unreliable, as discrete representations with substantially larger errors can achieve better understanding. Instead, the effective bit budget of discrete indices emerges as a key determinant of downstream performance. However, existing quantizers eventually saturate as additional codebooks contribute progressively less semantic information. As one approach to alleviating this saturation, we introduce Factorized Vector Quantization, which quantizes complementary, fixed-dimensional views of the visual feature with symmetric parallel codebooks. It continues to improve at larger bit budgets, ultimately matching continuous visual representations in multimodal understanding. Trained on industrial-scale multimodal data, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models, outperforming UniAR and Emu3-Chat by 22.8% and 59.2%, respectively, on a nine-metric average. To our knowledge, it is also the first discrete-representation model competitive with strong continuous-representation models such as Qwen3-VL, including on fine-grained OCR tasks. We further identify the key principles and a practical recipe enabling this competitiveness. These results and insights support the potential of discrete visual representations to underpin large-scale native multimodal foundation models. Code and models are available at https://github.com/hustvl/FVQ

title: Pushing Dexterity and Safety for In-Hand Object Pose Reaching That Works Remarkably Well
abstract: Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands is the next frontier of robotics, yet learned hand skills remain limited to simple grasps or basic repeated motions, such as rotating an object. As robots attempt more demanding in-hand maneuvers, safety, such as not dropping the object, becomes critical, yet it is rarely measured. We study in-hand object pose reaching, a task that demands diverse and difficult grasps: moving an object to almost any position and orientation within reach of the fingers, at any wrist orientation, through long sequences of consecutive goals. We present a recipe for training such policies for a LEAP hand in simulation without human data, built on a range of insights, from diverse resets and goals via generated grasp datasets to an adaptive friction curriculum. With careful system identification, the policies transfer zero-shot to the real hand, using either motion capture or a single wrist-mounted depth camera, and prove remarkably capable and robust. On top of the task policy, we add a learned residual safety filter with adjustable conservativeness, letting us tune the balance between performance and safety and greatly reduce object drops. In 13.3 hours of real-robot evaluation over 4,800 unseen goals across 4 objects and diverse wrist orientations, the state-based policy reaches 95.2% of goals within 2 cm and 0.4 rad, and the filter cuts its drops by 75% while still reaching 91.5% of goals. The policies can also spin a lightbulb held in an arbitrary pose, reach out-of-distribution goals, withstand fast arm motion and perturbations, and, needing only a wrist camera, serve as portable skills such as screwing in a lightbulb. We release the full recipe as a platform for studying performance, reliability, and safety in high-dimensional dexterous systems. Videos and more are available at https://ian-chuang.github.io/dexsafe/.

title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?
abstract: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.
